item.content:encoded:
German studio Sauerbruch Hutton and US practice Studio Gang have been selected to redesign German House to reflect the nation's values and create a "civic landmark" just north of the United Nations complex in Manhattan.

Selected by a jury, the redesign will see the recladding and interior redesign of the 325-foot-tall (99-metre-tall) skyscraper, which was originally designed by American studio SLCE Architects in the 1990s and serves as a base of operations for the Consulate General of the Federal Republic of Germany.

Sauerbruch Hutton and Studio Gang, design architect and architect of record, respectively, conceived a structure with bands of colour on the facade, brightening the current grey exterior.

The studios are combining civic presence and technical efficiency to "display the latest German engineering in sustainable construction before a global audience", according to the team.

"We look forward to working with the Bundesbau Baden-Württemberg and Sauerbruch Hutton to help reimagine German House as a more welcoming and sustainable model for civic architecture in New York and within the international diplomatic community," said Studio Gang founding partner Jeanne Gang.

"This project, which holds cultural exchange at its heart, is an exciting opportunity to bring together German design expertise with the proven project delivery in New York City."

The team plans to integrate photovoltaic panels onto the facade while formulating a box-window system that allows for solar shading and the opening of windows to allow for natural ventilation.

These interventions will be made while maintaining the heightened security necessary for a high-profile diplomatic building.

The team also plans to revamp the interior spaces, integrating a "sky lobby with a vertical garden" at mid-tower, which will serve as a meeting point for the Consulate General and the UN mission.

Read:

Eero Saarinen's Black Rock skyscraper refurbished in New York

A restaurant on the upper floors will open onto a shaded garden space.

The choice of renovating, as opposed to building new, was also highlighted by the studios, which noted the carbon benefits of preserving the structure.

"Through careful transformation rather than replacement, the tower is adapted to encourage exchange across departments while extending the life of the building for decades to come," said Sauerbruch Hutton partner Lina Lahiri.

The building will be the first project by Sauerbruch Hutton in the United States.

Other recent Manhattan skyscraper renovations include SOM's renovation of the iconic Lever House and Vocon Architects and MdeAS Architects' renovation of Eero Saarinen's Black Rock skyscraper.

The images are by ArtefactoryLab.

item.content:encoded:
New York architecture studio Diller Scofidio + Renfro has spliced an 1894 brick warehouse building with several glazed volumes to create a home for MIT's School of Architecture and Planning.

The Metropolitan Storage Warehouse building (MET) is located on the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) campus in Cambridge, Massachusetts and will house several architecture and design schools, including the Department of Architecture and the Department of Urban Studies and Planning.

The schools will relocate to the converted warehouse from their current location in the neoclassical Building 7, which sits cady corner to the new building.

Originally built in 1894 by local architect Frederic Pope and expanded throughout the decades, the brick warehouse once stored items such as pianos, carriages and furs for Boston's wealthiest families.

The studio's renovation included expanding the building's low ceiling heights and inserting "a series of carved-out voids" along the building's length, while maintaining portions of the original brick facade.

The project included careful "cutting strategies" and the application of new support systems to shift existing loads within the building to make room for modern academic spaces such as studios and makerspaces.

"By creating the necessary high-ceiling studio spaces through the removal of portions of the heavy, archaic masonry floor system, the structural load imposed on the existing columns and wood piles was significantly reduced," said Diller Scofidio + Renfro (DS+R).

"This reduction revealed sufficient reserve capacity within the existing structure to support the newly introduced, lightweight modern floor slabs, which are 'hung' by steel straps from beams supported by the existing columns and wood piles."

This architectural surgery allowed for a light, open, majority column-free interior and was informed by the interventions of Gordon Matta-Clark, according to the studio.

On the interior, the studio left some of the cuttings exposed to showcase the historical cross-sections to students. This can be seen in the sections of the original brick archways that run underneath the floor slabs.

Read:

MIT researchers design Heirloom House concrete components to last "1,000 years"

The programming and studios are now organised around large, double-height spaces, which are traversed via a continuous linear public stair.

They are organised into "neighbourhoods" across the five interconnected volumes of the building. Along one facade of the building, the glass insertions are exposed, while the other side is completely brick.

The studio also maintained details such as the building's fortress-like corner towers and crenellated corbeled cornices, while punching new windows into its two-foot-thick walls.

The team is targeting LEED Gold for the project.

"The techniques used in this adaptive reuse project have a pedagogical objective  –  to expose layers of history and allow students to experience firsthand the possibilities of breathing new life into a relic previously thought to be uninhabitable," said the studio.

DS+R recently adapted a London hangar into a publicly accessible storage facility for the Victoria and Albert Museum in London and is also working on a mass timber building at Boston University.

item.content:encoded:
Indian studio AKSH Architects has completed The Earthen Retreat, a cluster of guesthouses in Pune created by repurposing several small abandoned buildings and coating them with mud and lime plaster.

The 557-square-metre plot was previously occupied by four site offices and storage units that had outlived their original purpose.

While maintaining the existing timber and steel structures of these units, AKSH Architects used natural materials to demonstrate how "forgotten infrastructure" can be transformed into "architecture with lasting cultural, environmental and experiential value".

"The design intervention was intentionally radical," the studio's founder Akash Shingvi told Dezeen.

"Every space was reshaped through sculptural forms, natural mud and lime-plastered surfaces, local materials and fluid spatial planning, making it almost impossible to recognise the original buildings," added Shingvi.

"Our intention was to create an experience that feels timeless, earthy and deeply connected to nature, where architecture is perceived through texture, light and emotion rather than ornamentation."

The four blocks, each of which is divided into two neighbouring guesthouses, are arranged symmetrically around a communal paved patio with a swimming pool at its centre.

Inside, each of The Earthen Retreat's guesthouses contains a bedroom and a bathroom that has been left partially open to the elements, sheltered by a bamboo canopy that allows light and air to filter through.

Read:

Eleena Jamil shades Malaysian guesthouse with bamboo and steel canopy

Textured, lime-plastered walls and ceilings envelop the rooms, finished in earthy shades of beige and dark green, and punctured by arched and curved openings.

Curved forms were also used for built-in benches that extend around half of the bedrooms to form bedside tables, as well as for the bathroom's large, oval-shaped bath and a curved opening into the shower.

Externally, each of the four units has been given a matching rough plaster finish, with their perimeters shaded by the deep overhang of the bamboo roofs above.

"Curved, organic forms replace rigid partitions, allowing movement through the cottage to feel fluid, intuitive and experiential," said Shingvi.

"Since the retreat sits in a tropical setting, it didn't feel right to introduce materials that looked overly refined or disconnected from the place," he added.

"We consciously worked with natural materials that were commonly available in the local context, such as bamboo, lime and mud plaster and timber," he added.

Other projects in India that have recently incorporated mud and earth into their material palette include Aurva Illam near Hyderabad, a home by studio Iki Builds designed to reflect the rocky character of the nearby Deccan Plateau, and the mud-walled Winterfell house, which is woven around existing trees in Tamil Nadu.

The photography is by Harsh Lunavat.

item.content:encoded:
British carmaker Jaguar has revealed a glimpse of its upcoming Type 01 electric car, which has a central divider and "on-demand" screens.

The recently released renders show the interior of Jaguar's Type 01 electric car, which will be the production version of the much-discussed Type 00 concept car that was first revealed in 2024.

Jaguar plans to unveil the car this October.

The renders show a sleek, modern interior divided by a central bar that runs the full length of the car. This makes the Type 01 a four-seat car with distinct seating areas for each of the passengers.

Another notable aspect of the interior is the lack of a giant, central screen – commonly seen in modern electric cars.

A small screen is mounted on the central division, while other "digital interfaces are intelligently applied for control on demand".

"Our holistic design philosophy translates the vehicle's exterior presence into a distinctive interior architecture," said Jaguar's chief interior designer Thomas Holden.

"In contrast to the horizontal interior design norm, we emphasise its dramatic longitudinal nature through the central spine – an architectural statement that creates four individual spaces," he continued.

"With authentic materials, technology on demand and reductive flowing surfaces, Type 01 presents unmistakable drama and theatre that will define the modern luxury automotive interior of the future."

A prototype of the Type 01 will be on display at this week's Monterey Car Week.

The car will be the first released by Jaguar as part of its "complete reset" as it moves to electric-only cars. The reset began with a controversial rebrand at the end of 2024.

Read:

Jaguar's controversial Type 00 concept car spotted driving on the streets of Paris

"Jaguar Type 01 is the first production car to follow our new creative philosophy," said Jaguar managing director Rawdon Glover.

"Unmistakable from every angle, the interior is no different. With Type 01, we wanted every journey to be an occasion, from how it drives to how it looks and how it makes you feel.

"With a confidence-inspiring GT driving position, clean and sophisticated technology and dramatic styling, Type 01 has an interior like no other."

The reset was led by Jaguar Land Rover chief creative officer Gerry McGovern, who departed the company at the end of 2025, a year after the unveiling of the radical Type 00 concept car.

item.content:encoded:
British eyewear brand Cubitts has unveiled its first shop in Manchester, designed by locally based studio Youth to reflect the city's industrial and musical history without resorting to the obvious.

Youth co-founders Oliver Collinge and Liam McGroarty planned the interior to reflect the present and future of the British city, with subtle references to the past rather than cliches.

It includes a shelving display combining tubular steel uprights with dapple-textured glass shelves, a faceted oak counter housing a till and record player, and a pair of figurative sandstone sculptures by artist Richard Perry.

The designers aimed to create a space "that feels both familiar and distinctly contemporary".

"Inspired by the city itself, the space draws on Manchester's culture and historic character, reinterpreted through a contemporary lens," they said.

The approach reflects the brief set by Cubitts founder Tom Broughton "to make the space feel distinctly Cubitts without resorting to the usual Manchester shorthand".

"It was important that Cubitts Manchester was designed in Manchester, and not just deposited here," Broughton said.

"Manchester does not need another London brand telling it how interesting it is. We're simply pleased to finally be here, and hope to make ourselves useful."

The store is located in Smithfield Buildings in the Northern Quarter, a collection of buildings that once housed the Affleck & Brown department store, dubbed the 'Harrods of the North'.

After more than a decade looking at locations, Broughton and his team chose this one for its history as a supplier of cloth and made-to-measure garments.

Read:

EBBA Architects transforms former jellied-eel restaurant into eyewear store

This aligns with Cubitts' own approach, with facilities for eye examinations, spectacle repairs and customisation made visible in the store.

"Smithfield Buildings felt immediately right: a spectacle shop inside a former draper's department store, in a neighbourhood shaped by making, music and independent trade," said Broughton.

Waxed cotton curtains softly divide different areas in tribute to Affleck & Brown's legacy, while other additions include a vintage revolving bookcase.

Produced by Manchester cabinetmakers Goodall, Lamb and Heighway, this century-old piece was made with salvaged timber from the Royal Navy ship HMS Foudroyant.

Artworks also hint at industrial production; a seamstress is depicted in a painting by artist Francis Hoyland, while a cubist gouache by artist Marcel Gille depicts a forge worker.

Completing the design are dimpled mirrors that offer slightly cloudy reflections and a collection of records spanning soul, jazz, punk and electronica.

Cubitts Manchester is the brand's 21st location, following others that include the peep-show-inspired Cubitts Soho and the art-deco-style Cubitts Leeds.

The company also just unveiled a new headquarters in London's King's Cross, in a historic building that began as a working stable for the Crosse & Blackwell Vinegar Works, before being converted into an office for a publishing house.

The photography is courtesy of Cubitts.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Kii has designed an ice cream shop on Miyakojima Island, Japan, featuring a pink ceiling, a limestone counter and perforated concrete tiles.

Called SR Ice Cream Miyakojima, the cafe and ice cream shop is located on an island in the southern part of Japan's Okinawa prefecture in the Pacific Ocean.

Its ocean-side setting influenced the interior, which features local materials chosen for their weather resistance.

"On Miyakojima Island, its local residents, new arrivals and tourists coexist and the goal was to create a welcoming environment where people of all backgrounds can simply drop by to enjoy a shared atmosphere over an ice cream or coffee," Kii co-founder Satoshi Arai told Dezeen.

"To withstand Miyakojima's subtropical oceanic climate, materials were also carefully selected to ensure finishes which are both functional and enduring," Arai continued.

The centrepiece of SR Ice Cream Miyakojima is a large, rounded counter made from limestone and with a lime plaster tabletop, around which customers can stand or sit.

Kii worked with an Okinawan plaster specialist to design the counter.

"Work to the counter involves applying rounded lumps of limestone clay – Ryukyu limestone, a local material in Miyakojima – to the counter surface one piece at a time," Kii co-founder Kei Nakatomi told Dezeen.

"The process of applying this material repeatedly creates a layered finish, and allows its unique texture to truly stand out," Nakatomi continued.

"The tabletop was also crafted using the same limestone clay and polished to reveal the material's unique texture."

Kii also inserted a playful arched door in the counter to create easy access for filter maintenance.

Above the central counter, Kii added a curved ceiling designed to draw visitors' attention and make the counter an attraction in itself.

Read:

Funamachi Base cafe and sweet shop designed as "extension of the park"

The studio chose a pale pink hue for the ceiling, in response to the natural light of the cafe's surroundings.

"Considering the dramatic shifts in natural light throughout the day on Miyakojima, we tested several options on-site to determine the ideal colour – ultimately selecting this specific shade of pink – to ensure it harmonised with the environment at any time of day or night," Arai said.

The salt air and harsh sunlight on the island influenced Arai and Nakatomi's choice of materials, and the two designers also aimed to showcase artisanal craftsmanship from different regions of Japan.

Apart from the limestone counter, one of the most noticeable materials in the SR ice cream shop is a specific type of concrete brick, which is perforated with holes for typhoon-struck areas.

"In the Okinawa area, where typhoons frequently hit, concrete blocks with holes are in use for architecture," Nakatomi said.

"When considering how to incorporate this unique characteristic of the region as an element that would blend seamlessly into the interior, custom tiles by Tajimi Tiles were selected."

The studio also added cushions woven from Cogon grass, which is native to the island, and colourful glazed stools by NOTA shop in Shigaraki – an old pottery area.

These pastel stools were specially chosen for the ice cream store as they had to be easy to maintain and have a non-directional design to fit under low tables.

"We picked the stool regularly produced by NOTA shop, with an original glazed colour on it," Arai said. "We designed these with the mindset of embracing the unpredictable results over its final appearance, and enjoyed the process of letting the results surprise us."

Kii did have some input into the glazing, as the studio wanted the stools to resemble ice cream that had started to melt.

"We did, however, go through a number of prototypes to fine-tune the glaze, aiming for a colour and texture that's reminiscent of melting ice cream," Arai added.

Overall, the studio said the ice cream shop, which sits on the ground floor of an ocean-side commercial development, has become the type of place that it envisioned when coming up with the design.

"We had heard that many guests would linger or stick around, whilst being engaged with guests inside or outside – just like a community, and as the type of space we had imagined while we had designed it," Nakatomi said.

Other Japanese cafes recently covered on Dezeen include a cafe and brewery on Teshima Island and a Blue Bottle Coffee cafe informed by Osaka Castle.

The photography is by Masanori Kaneshita.

item.content:encoded:
Texas architecture studio Clayton Korte has completed a Corten steel-clad structure for storing vineyard equipment at a winery on the Central Coast of California.

The 4,315-square-foot (400-square-metre) barn serves a 150-acre vineyard in Cayucos, a town in California's Santa Lucia Range. The barn sits between a working Syrah vineyard to the west and an oak forest to the east.

A simple plan with a gabled roof, the structure serves as a mediator between cultivated and natural landscapes.

"The structure opens westward with broad bays that frame the vineyard and tie the building directly to the daily rhythm of harvest and cultivation, while the forested hillside grounds it to the east," Clayton Korte principal Brian Korte told Dezeen.

The plan is organised around functionality for farm operations. Sliding doors at each end allow for easy mobility, while five bay doors open for manoeuvring equipment and work as cover for a generous porch area for outdoor work.

To accommodate the rural, off-grid site for wildfire, the studio clad the wood-framed structure entirely in weathering steel – corrugated on the roof and long sides and smooth on the short sides – that will resist fires, age gracefully and reduce long-term maintenance.

"Materials for a barn need to be practical, robust and not too precious, while also bringing their own authenticity and simple elegance to a structure," Korte said.

"They are honest and perform the dual task of serving both structural requirements and architectural finishes in many cases."

"The foggy marine layer that rolls through this landscape becomes part of the architecture, deepening the steel's natural patina over time so the building settles into, rather than stands apart from, the vineyards and hillsides around it."

Mesh screens extend out of the gabled ends, finishing out the building's profile with a translucent film and complementing the sliding doors that were salvaged from the local Saxum Winery.

Inside, the wooden frame and raw plywood panelling were left exposed to allow for the building's use to be adapted over time, and the fluted-glazed overhead doors provide an unexpected detail to the agricultural structure, washing the interior in daylight while keeping the form simple and utilitarian.

Read:

Clayton Korte creates "familiar yet exclusive" winery buildings in California

"In a project like this, it's the small moves that matter most – subtle shifts in orientation, material transitions and moments of openness that create a deeper dialogue with the land," said Clayton Korte senior architect Josh Nieves.

"Nothing is loud, but everything is deliberate."

Operating entirely off-grid, the barn's photovoltaic panels charge an on-site battery bank that manages lighting and power for operations, eliminating any reliance on external utilities.

"Sustainability isn't just about systems – it's about restraint and respect," Korte said.

"By building off the grid, using reclaimed elements and allowing materials to weather naturally, we let the structure quietly support the land rather than compete with it."

Clayton Korte, which has offices in Austin and San Antonio and was formerly known as Clayton & Little, has worked on wineries across California and Texas.

In the last few years, the 25-person studio has completed a pair of polycarbonate and steel buildings for Fulldraw Vineyard and a breezy, weathering steel barn for the Saxum Vineyard, both in Paso Robles, California, as well as a wine cave embedded in limestone outside of Austin.

The photography is by Casey Dunn and Ray Castro.

Dezeen School Shows: modular housing designed for communities affected by the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires is among projects from UCLA.

Also featured is a housing program to support first-time buyers and a project exploring flood mitigation for a lake in California, USA.

UCLA

Institution: UCLA
School: UCLA Architecture and Urban Design
Courses: Master of Architecture, Master of Science in Architecture and Urban Design and Bachelor of Arts in Architectural Studies, MA and PhD
Tutors: Hitoshi Abe, Cristóbal Amunátegui, Kutan Ayata, Khorshid Azad, Hallie Black, Miroslava Brooks, Morgane Copp, Salmaan Craig, Dana Cuff, Kevin Daly, Neil Denari, Liam Denhamer, Samaa Elimam, Yara Feghali, Claus Benjamin Freyinger, Georgina Huljich, Mariana Ibañez, Jeffrey Inaba, Julia Koerner, Max Kuo, Ayala Levin, Todd Lynch, Greg Lynn, Narineh Mirzaeian, Michael Osman, Güvenç Özel, Martin Paull, Jason Payne, Michael Peguero, Heather Roberge, Natasha Sandmeier, Mohamed Sharif and Tucker van Leuwen-Hall

School statement:

"UCLA Architecture and Urban Design's exceptional faculty teaches students to engage in the world around them, to see ideas as productive forms of response and to leverage design and writing as expressions of newly curated perspectives.

"Through rigorous inquiry, we interrogate contemporary urban issues and propose possible futures with equal measures of expertise, optimism and vision.

"These ideas are grounded in a critical engagement with the history and theory of architecture and the future contingencies of contemporary culture and an engagement with the geographic, cultural and urban contexts of Los Angeles and Southern California."

Medium by Nathan Logan

"As a sprawling urban fabric with pockets of high density and miles of single-family homes in between, Los Angeles has struggled to develop medium-rise, multi-unit housing that is both architecturally compelling and effective in adding density to the city.

“Medium activates the 'mid' to be a space of novelty and dignity rather than a compromised middle ground.

"Chains of mini-towers delicately emerge from the ground and can span lengths in the air to minimise impact on sites. Short spurts of verticality bring interior unit proportions that are less familiar to LA but well represented abroad.

"As an adaptable and re-configurable design, 'Medium' could exist anywhere, yet aims to exist in the spaces Los Angeles underutilises and work around the conditions that make building housing here challenging and normative."

Student: Nathan Logan
Course: Research Studio: Future [Hi]stories of the City
Tutor: Kutan Ayata

Building-Like Non-Buildings by Nabil Davidson and Zirui Wang

"For over a century, the Refinery in Los Angeles has converted crude oil into the fuel that powers the city, producing a second landscape beneath it: a thick, inaccessible region built from building-like non-buildings that sustain the city while remaining concealed within it.

"Originating from this contradiction, Building-Like Non-Buildings accepts the contaminated, the imperfect, the uninhabitable space of the city as the substance of the site, and rejects the myth of the tabula rasa that requires a clean ground or a blank slate.

"The project proposes that the Refinery's long-term environmental remediation should not remain a hidden engineering operation, but become an architectural project unfolding over sixty years, transforming the refinery into a landscape of ecological monitoring, repair and public space through episodes of documenting, analysing and building."

Students: Nabil Davidson and Zirui Wang
Course: Research Studio: Future [Hi]stories of the City
Tutor: Kutan Ayata

Salton's Life Raft by Hunter Blackwell and Brandt Rentel

"The Salton Sea faces several increasingly certain futures: continued evaporation, toxic dust from its exposed lakebed and the rapid expansion of geothermal energy and lithium extraction.

"Residents, from artists and agricultural workers to engineers and off-grid communities, experience these changes differently, yet many share a belief that lithium could bring investment, renewal or rescue.

"In a region shaped by cost-driven development, however, its environmental crises are more likely to be managed through technical solutions, such as dust suppression and brine management, than through any broader reimagining of place. What role, then, can architecture play?

"The articulation of form in the shared architecture of optimism, fear, and futility is an ark: not as practical infrastructure, but as a vessel for collective myth.

"Drawing on ancient flood narratives in which arks have taken many forms, from coracles and cubes to rectangular hulls, this ark shifts from a handheld artefact to a megastructure along the Salton Sea's shore.

"The ark materialises the region's competing fears and hopes: ecological collapse, industrial transformation, salvation and futility. Sometimes the flood never comes, but when it does, the people and their efforts are vindicated."

Students: Hunter Blackwell and Brandt Rentel
Course: Research Studio: Future [Hi]stories of the City
Tutor: Kutan Ayata

Los Angeles Generics: Post-Aesthetics of the Mundane by Peter Cheng and EmaLee Davidson

"This project investigates a built project through post-construction evidence, documenting an anonymous block in the backdrop of Los Angeles.

"The block serves as the site for translating, tracking, and testing Los Angeles' cultural influence on vernacular aesthetics. Solutions of the past adapt and transform themselves for new purposes, estranging familiar material logics.

"The project, therefore, includes recurring conditions from Los Angeles: details, drawing sets, finish systems and photographic documentation that register the distance between intended form and built form.

"In a post-Los Angeles aesthetic era where palm trees are no longer found and new iconics are frowned upon, this project demands attention to how new languages are still formed through an evolution of recollections.

"In this sense, it neither recreates the past nor falls into nostalgic preservation, but treats mundane architecture of Los Angeles as an evidentiary archive translating the design of a single block into a new architectural proposition."

Students: Peter Cheng and EmaLee Davidson
Course: Research Studio, Future [Hi]stories of the City
Tutor: Kutan Ayata

LA 2066: Preserving the Image by Areeba Naeem and Alanis Velazquez

"LA 2066: Preserving the Image reimagines architectural preservation in Los Angeles, where cultural value is increasingly tied to recognisability rather than material permanence.

"Responding to redevelopment pressures, the project proposes a new preservation framework that treats architecture as transferable visual and spatial identity.

"Preservation is no longer about freezing a building in time. Instead, it becomes a way of shaping perception.

"Rather than reconstructing buildings, culturally significant sites are preserved either as volumetric voids embedded within new developments or as recognisable fragments redistributed across the city.

"These strategies transform preservation from a static act into an active system of cultural continuity, where memory is held through absence, perception and image rather than physical fabric.

"By preserving only a building's minimum recognisable identity, the project challenges conventional notions of authenticity and proposes a new architecture of controlled absence."

Students: Areeba Naeem and Alanis Velazquez
Course: Research Studio: Future [Hi]stories of the City
Tutor: Kutan Ayata

Floresomatic by Anjana George and Ceren Harputoglu

"Floresomatic proposes a new housing paradigm in which digital intelligence, urban agriculture and human experience are synthesised into a single cyber-physical architectural system.

"The project operates as a cyber-physical farming engine that integrates sensory feedback, embodiment and spatial interaction. Residents engage directly with plant life through immersive environments where biological processes are translated into tactile and perceptual experiences.

"Domestic life is organised as a participatory ecological system structured through gamified interactions. Residents cultivate high-value plant species that function simultaneously as biological entities and augmented interfaces, prompting care, maintenance and collaboration.

"In this way, housing becomes a collective metabolic process, where individual contributions directly shape environmental performance and community outcomes.

"By positioning farming as a central spatial and social driver, the project reframes domestic space as a site of collective production, learning and environmental awareness."

Students: Anjana George and Ceren Harputoglu
Course: MSAUD Architectural Intelligence Studio, 'Automated Abundance'
Tutors: Güvenç Özel and Michael Peguero

Campus Massima: Interventions on UCLA's Drake Stadium and Sproul Hall by Borna Torabinejad, Miriam Alghanim, Feihao Ye, Xiangshu Zheng and Jiaying Liang

"'Campus Massima' is the culmination of a year-long research initiative exploring the intersections of biomimicry, material innovation and additive manufacturing.

"Rather than executing a single architectural object, the project documents a rigorous evolution of design – from micro-scale material experiments and wearable prototypes to meso-scale structural components, ultimately resolving in macro-scale urban interventions on the UCLA campus ahead of the 2028 Summer Olympics.

"By studying the cellular structures and systems of marine organisms, the team developed a foundational design language.

"These wearable prototypes served as a testing ground for translating biological principles into structural geometry and fabrication strategies.

"Extensive material testing – including printing on fabric, flexible TPU systems, silicone casting and embedded inserts – defined the boundaries of material behaviour."

Students: Borna Torabinejad, Miriam Alghanim, Feihao Ye, Xiangshu Zheng and Jiaying Liang
Course: MSAUD Material Innovations Studio: Towards Circular, Innovative Buildings for the Olympics
Tutors: Julia Koerner and Tucker van Leuwen-Hall

Rock n Roll by Sara Kaplan, Keily Sarica and Ellie Wiygul

"The project is organised into three zones: high-density living, mid-density living and art/studio space, with communal programs suspended between them in section.

"Moving left to right, the scheme transitions from a dense, rigid residential mass aligned to the grid into increasingly open creative work environments.

"Density becomes both a formal and social ambition, shaping the structure’s circulation and collective life. Between these zones, a constructed interior landscape takes shape as a canyon of dirt and rock exposed to light, creating an environmental ecology within the building that supports both living and working.

"The structural and sectional system proposes a tectonic logic that is openly machine-like, unconventional in its resolution and legible as a mechanism.

"Designed for a range of inhabitants, from commuters needing only a few hours of rest to permanent families, the project uses a disciplined modular unit system capable of absorbing diverse needs without sacrificing organisational clarity."

Students: Sara Kaplan, Keily Sarica and Ellie Wiygul
Course: Undergraduate Studio, "Off-Campus Living"
Tutor: Claus Benjamin Freyinger

Individually Together by Camila Gomez

"This project proposes a community land trust-based program for groups of young professionals looking to get their start at 'individually living together' as first-time home buyers.

"Units are designed in parallel clusters, a primary and an ADU, allowing for purchase of single or conjoined residences.

"A walkway 'skewer' connects all three clusters, coalescing them into a collective housing complex. All main entrances, with the exception of two JADUs, are located along the raised skewer.

"These, alongside pockets of terraces and open space, incentivise heavy use of the skewer. Each north face opens using perforated accordion louvres, creating opportunities for semi-exterior kitchens and terraces."

Student: Camila Gomez
Course: First-year MArch Core Studio, "Housing Los Angeles: Reframing the Dream"
Tutor: Yara Feghali

Courtyard Commons by Shun Ying Zhuang

"Courtyard Commons reimagines collective housing in Los Angeles through a layered network of homes, courtyards and shared outdoor space.

"The project is organised into four residential lots, each pairing a primary residence with an ADU or JADU to accommodate diverse household structures, changing family needs and multigenerational living.

"Two shared courtyards form the collective heart of the development, creating spaces for everyday encounters, informal gathering and community life.

"At the scale of each lot, a backyard provides a more intimate outdoor retreat shared by the primary residence and ADU.

"A clear diagonal circulation spine links the courtyards, homes and thresholds across the site, establishing a gradual transition between public, collective and private domains.

"Drawing from the tradition of Los Angeles courtyard housing, the project explores how home is not defined by a single dwelling, but emerges through relationships, shared occupation and the spaces in between."

Student: Shun Ying Zhuang
Course: First-year MArch Core Studio, "Housing Los Angeles: Reframing the Dream"
Tutor: Miroslava Brooks

Interstitial Skies by Sydney Patterson and Mengyan Wang

"Interstitial Skies reimagines the existing 1334 Lincoln Boulevard structure in Venice, California as a site of vertical ascension and atmospheric lightness.

"We preserve the original building proportions while introducing a mirrored, staggered counterpart to establish a formal dialogue of slipping and veiling.

"This shifting geometry drives our distributed sectional logic; rather than providing a singular ground-level lobby, we thread architectural stairs throughout the project to create 'floating lobbies'. These spaces pull the civic energy of the street upward.

"A steel frame with concrete cores achieves the structural agility necessary for the airiness of floor plates and section. A transfer slab at the ground level grounds this lightness, a move that enables the performance hall to occupy the lower level while liberating the floors above for the slipping and stacking of educational programming.

"The building's envelope acts as a diaphanous veil and, through a rhythm of elevational strata, translucency and stepping profile; the facade is a responsive skin that tracks the internal floor plate slippage.

"This system links the idea of brightness to the performance of the building, where the architecture itself becomes as ephemeral and dynamic as the Santa Monica sky."

Students: Sydney Patterson and Mengyan Wang
Course: Second-year MArch Core Studio, "Next – Cycle"
Tutor: Narineh Mirzaeian

BNSF Intermodal Runway by Kay Wright

"The BNSF Intermodal Runway plan is the proposal for a new airport in Los Angeles, sited at the intersection of Vernon and Commerce, California.

"The building is a 1,000-foot-long, six-story structure, including two levels of airport space and four levels of a thickened reading room.

"This project suggests an offbeat strategy for the planning and architecture of terminals, runways, public institutions and transportation in Southern California."

Student: Kay Wright
Course: First-year MArch Core Studio, "Housing Los Angeles: Reframing the Dream"
Tutor: Jeffrey Inaba

Music School for Youth Orchestra Los Angeles by Alanis Baez and Anna Shoemaker

"This project extends the mission of YOLA (Youth Orchestra Los Angeles) into the city, arguing that cultural space and artistic opportunity are civic resources that belong within the public realm.

"The architecture is organised into three distinct elements: the plinth, the agora and the jewel. Each element follows its own structural logic, optimising seismic performance while expressing the project as three interdependent architectural movements.

"The communal nature of music is made visible through sound, movement, and gathering, allowing the life of the school to engage the surrounding neighbourhood."

"A continuous perforated aluminium screen wraps both the existing structure and the new addition, dissolving the boundary between old and new into a unified plinth.

"Above the plinth, the performance hall, or the 'jewel', appears suspended, separated by a minimal glass curtain wall that emphasises the contrast between the grounded base and the floating volume.

"Clad in high-gloss glazed terracotta tiles, the jewel cantilevers over the existing structure, acknowledging it without fully touching it.

"This conceptual independence is reinforced structurally: the hall is supported by transfer beams and cantilevered trusses independent of the plinth below, while the base relies on steel columns, reinforced concrete walls and waffle slabs."

Students: Alanis Baez and Anna Shoemaker
Course: Second-year MArch Core Studio, "Next – Cycle"
Tutor: Georgina Huljich

Cultural Anchors in Altadena by Jessie Zhao and Bella Zheng

"Altadena was one of the communities ravaged by the January 2025 wildfires in the Los Angeles area.

"'Cultural Anchors in Altadena' proposes modular units to resolve a major dilemma that arises in the regeneration of communities after disaster.

"Typically, quickly securing housing is essential to community regeneration. However, this often results in a dry, top-down approach to housing development, one that can become an obstacle to building a rich community for the future.

"On the other hand, if development is allowed to take more time, residents may leave, risking the collapse of the community altogether.

"This proposal for Altadena is to first rapidly concentrate a large number of modular units at a single site in the disaster-affected area to provide temporary housing, and then, in stages, relocate the units from that dense cluster of buildings to gradually develop the community as a whole into a richer living environment.

"Through this compelling strategy of 'rapidly building a dense structure, then gradually breaking it apart to develop a rich environment distributed across the area,' residents can return to their own land immediately, engage in dialogue about the future shape of their community's regeneration as they live together, and gradually carry out development aimed at the future."

Students: Jessie Zhao and Bella Zheng
Course: Architecture of Mobility
Tutor: Hitoshi Abe

Architecture studio HNTB has unveiled the design of an 18,000-seat arena in Plano, Texas, for the Dallas Stars NHL team.

Set to be built as part of a wider "year-round district", the arena will be the permanent home for the Dallas Stars National Hockey League (NHL) team.

The area will be located alongside the Dallas North Tollway, around 20 miles north of its current home in the American Airlines Center in Downtown Dallas.

Few details of the arena have been announced, with renderings showing an irregularly shaped venue embedded behind by mid-rise blocks.

"The most memorable arenas become part of the identity of a city and its people," said HNTB chief design officer Ryan Gedney.

"Our goal is to create a home that is unmistakably rooted in the identity of the Dallas Stars, one that captures the passion and intensity of hockey while reflecting the unique character and culture of north Texas."

The arena forms the centrepiece of a wider development of mid-rise buildings along with a taller office tower.

HNTB expressed how integrating the team into the community was a key part of the design strategy.

Read:

Eight record-breaking stadiums from the biggest to the most expensive

"Great arenas create unforgettable moments, but the very best become places that communities embrace every day of the year," said Gedney.

"By seamlessly integrating the arena with an active, year-round district, we have an opportunity to establish a new benchmark for how sports, entertainment and community come together to create lasting value for fans, the franchise and the region."

The Dallas Stars is the latest US sports team to announce plans to create a new home, with NFL team Kansas City Chiefs recently releasing plans for a 70,000-seat stadium designed by Manica and the Washington Commanders are planning a colonnaded stadium design by HKS.

item.content:encoded:
US-based studio Pelli Clarke & Partners has created a museum, with a futuristic bridge and tower embedded with wind turbines, dedicated to artist Lola Mora in Argentina.

Sited on a forested hillside on the edge of a suburban development in San Salvador de Jujuy in northwestern Argentina, the Lola Mora Cultural Centre was purpose-built to house the late artist's sculpture.

It is also significant as the final project led by Pelli Clarke & Partners founder César Pelli, who died in 2019.

The building has aspects of both the space-age and a more organic modern sensibility, with sheer white walls and glass in some places and rough-hewed stones in others.

Its main structure is teardrop-shaped in plan, with an elongated entry along a bridge that leads into a wide gallery space.

This bridge helps the structure navigate the topography, crossing a ravine that comes into the middle of the site.

Affixed outside are rounded structures clad in stone that feature auxiliary functions such as restaurants, libraries and gift shops.

The juxtaposition of the building's two material languages is best seen at the entryway.

Jutting out from over the door that leads to the bridge is a cantilevered, white overhang.

To the right of the entry is one of the stone-clad structures with the name of the institution featured prominently in cut metal letters.

One of the other oblong structures is attached to the main structure in the middle of the bridge, sitting at the crest of the ravine, and the other is adjacent to the fanned gallery volume itself.

The landscaping navigates the site, connecting the structures to a series of paths and gardens, carried out by Balmori Associates, a studio founded by César Pelli's late wife, Diana Balmori.

Pelli Clarke & Partners highlighted the sustainable aspects of the building, which it claims generates 100 per cent of its power on site, mostly through the arrays of photovoltaic panels on the roofs of all the structures.

A tower near the centre of the site "signals the cultural center's presence from afar" and features elegantly wrapped wind turbines that provide additional power to the facilities.

The studio also sited the insulation and rainwater-gathering systems as well as the sourcing of local stone, reducing transport emissions, as sustainable factors in the building, which it claims operates at net-zero energy usage.

While the building subtly signals its energy goals with that tower, it is ultimately a purpose-built structure for six monumental sculptures by Mora, which were previously outside.

The six sculptures feature along the floor-to-ceiling glass of the primary gallery space, which looks out at the forests, mountains and river beyond. Other works were placed in an interior structure in the middle of the gallery that was clad in dark-stained wood slats.

This interior structure provides a light-controlled space to showcase smaller works and works that utilise artificial light sources, and has a back-lit oculus in its ceiling.

Read:

Pelli Clarke & Partners completes Japan's tallest skyscraper in Tokyo

Throughout the gallery spaces, the interior architecture is minimalistic, with smooth wooden floors and white walls.

In the auxiliary spaces, the ceilings were kept low with more backlit ceiling lighting and different window and flooring configurations depending on use. The library space has carpet and thin horizontal windows, while the restaurant has wooden flooring akin to the gallery and horizontal bar windows.

According to Rafael Pelli, who serves as a partner at the studio, the site and purpose of the building had particular significance to his father, César Pelli, who was born in northwestern Argentina.

And though the studio has projects worldwide, it is its first cultural building in the country.

"As one of César Pelli's final projects, the opening of the Lola Mora Cultural Center in San Salvador de Jujuy is both a professional and personal honor for our firm and my family," said Rafael Pelli.

"My father, a native of the Argentine northwest, admired Lola Mora's work from a young age. To create a space that celebrates and carries forward her legacy, in a community so close to my heart, is a true privilege."

Other recently completed projects by Pelli Clarke & Partners include a Boston skyscraper that "reshapes the skyline" on top of a historic building and Mexico City's tallest skyscraper.

item.content:encoded:
Belgium studio OYO Architects has built a steel-framed office above a warehouse in Ostend, Belgium, to create an operations centre for energy company Elia.

Designed to evoke the offshore platforms used by Elia for electricity generation, the service centre in Ostend port has two distinct elements for its two functions – warehouse and offices.

OYO Architects designed the large warehouse, workshop and service area as a long monolithic concrete block stretching along the harbourside.

Rather than placing the offices as an upper storey stretching the length of the building, the studio raised a three-storey block on steel columns above the warehouse.

Raising the block above the warehouse gave the offices a view across the docks, while also creating a visible landmark for the company.

"Our design concept strategically separates the primary functions, achieving a pure and maximally functional design," said the studio.

Read:

MAD crowns Fenix museum in Rotterdam with "living room for people"

"The structure comprises a massive monolith and a landmark office building in a steel structure, acting as a beacon in the landscape," it continued.

"This approach aligns with Elia's desire for a both aesthetically pleasing and functionally optimised building that resonates with the company's DNA."

The lower two floors contain open-plan office space for the power company, along with a control room and meeting spaces, while a visitor centre and viewpoint occupies the upper storey.

The red steel structure is visible throughout the office spaces, which have floor-to-ceiling windows, and surrounding the building on all sides is a steel walkway that acts as a wrap-around balcony.

Throughout the project, the studio aimed to evoke the maritime nature of Elia's activities.

Along with the offshore-platform appearance of the office block, the precast concrete cladding panels of the warehouse were cast on a sand bed to give a rippled effect.

Reused and recycled maritime materials were used internally, with several old sea buoys converted into entrance lights by designer Re-volt. Office carpets were made from recycled fishing nets, while acoustic panels were made from seagrass and side tables incorporated seashells.

Overall, OYO Architects aimed to create a "high-performance machine" that reflected, but did not directly imitate, the energy company's highly technical marine operations.

"The service centre is conceived as a rational and flexible hangar, functioning as a high-performance machine," said the studio.

"Functional and easily accessible entrances lead to an open hall at the heart of the design, offering a functional connection to the program on both sides."

Other recent Belgian projects on Dezeen include a contemporary design exhibition in a neo-gothic villa and the winner of the Mies van der Rohe award.

item.content:encoded:
A campaign has been launched to turn the V&A Dundee by Japanese architect Kengo Kuma into Lego's first Scottish building set.

The campaign follows the creation of a 2,900-piece model replica of the local landmark by founder of web studio 532 Design Brian McNicoll.

The small-scale replica, which is currently on show within the museum, has been submitted to the Danish toy brand's Ideas platform where people vote for fan-built prototypes to be developed into official sets.

A total of 10,000 supporters are required for the design to be reviewed for production by Lego's board.

If successful, the V&A Dundee would become the first Scottish building in Lego's architecture range.

The campaign is being backed by Kuma, who said the Lego set of the museum, which was his first UK building, would introduce the building to "people all over the world".

"It's an honour to see my building recreated in Lego and I'm impressed with how well Brian has translated the design," the architect said.

"I always wanted the building to be a gate through which the city can connect with the world, reflecting Dundee's once thriving global trade routes on the river," Kuma continued.

"If this design becomes an official Lego set, then people all over the world will be building a Dundee landmark."

Read:

Lego reveals Sagrada Familia set to celebrate Gaudí centenary

Perched on the city's waterfront, the museum was completed by Kuma in 2018 as an outpost of London's V&A museum and has since become a local landmark.

Its structure was designed in reference the city's coastal landscape and is formed of two angular volumes clad in 2,500 precast concrete panels arranged in horizontal bands.

According to McNicoll, the building's architectural quality renders it particularly suited to being rebuilt in Lego, for which he drew closely on photographs and 3D visuals of the museum.

"This model captures the angular design and textured facade of the V&A Museum Dundee," said McNicoll.

"That banded, angular facade is what makes the building so unusually well suited to being rebuilt in Lego," he continued.

"I used a 3D version of the museum inside a Dundee Waterfront app to check scale and angles from every side as I built, rotating it like a reference photo you can walk around."

The campaign, which has seen support from local schools and garnered over 2,800 votes so far, will run until next year.

"It's a joy to see the city get behind the project, especially so many school children, and I hope the support continues until it reaches 10,000 votes," Kuma added.

Lego recently unveiled the Sagrada Familia set, which is its largest one yet with 12,060 pieces. It also created a giant World Cup trophy in New York from 1.3 million bricks to mark this year's tournament.

The photography is by Brian McNicoll.

item.content:encoded:
Antwerp-based gallery Uppercut is presenting the works of six contemporary designers in the ornate halls and salons of a neo-gothic villa near Bruges.

Elaborate glass vessels by Danish designer Alexander Kirkeby and melted polystyrene furniture by French designer Nicolas Zanoni are among the pieces on show inside the rooms of the 19th-century Chateau de Spycker in Sint-Kruis.

The exhibition, titled God Speed, also features pieces by Belgian designer Linde Freya Tangelder, South Korean designer Yoon Shun, New York-based Greek designer Kiki Goti and LS Gomma, the studio of British designer Joel Muggleton.

The is the fourth annual summer exhibition that Uppercut has staged at Chateau de Spycker since director Scott Lippens founded the gallery in 2023.

Originally the summer residence of an aristocratic family, the villa was bought by Lippens' family nearly 20 years ago and has been operating as guesthouse since a renovation by his mother, fashion buyer Caroline Grootaert.

While previous shows were limited to a single room, this time Uppercut's exhibition extends through from the grand entry hall into the dining and drawing rooms.

In each space, contemporary works are in dialogue with period details that include decorative wall mouldings, gilded furniture, marble fireplaces and antique artworks.

Lippens said the approach was inspired by the newly inaugurated Fondazione Dries Van Noten in Venice, with which he had some involvement.

"I realised I could leave a lot of the antiquities in here and embrace the way they clash with the contemporary design," he said. "They actually go really well together."

The juxtaposition is particularly apparent in the dining room, where LS Gomma's Drunken Vessels, made from metal mesh and PU rubber, are displayed on the table alongside figurative sculptures.

For the drawing room, a space dominated by green walls and colourful textiles, Zanoni's multitextural furniture is arranged over patterned rugs, while Goti's hand-blown glass vases adorn a marble-topped console table.

The balance tips more towards contemporary in the entry hall, where most of the large works are on show.

There are various pieces by Tangelder, founder of the studio Destroyers/Builders, including her folded aluminium Reworked bench and a coffee table on which Kirkeby's glassware is presented.

Shun has also contributed various pieces, including both lighting and furniture, which demonstrate his particular methods of handcarving and charring oak.

Lippens said the gallery focuses on designers who specialise in material processes.

"Maybe it comes from my fashion background, but I'm very material-driven," he told Dezeen.

The gallerist originally studied fashion design, but moved into the world of collectible design when a side-hustle of buying and selling vintage mid-century furniture gained traction.

Uppercut evolved out of this, as Lippens became increasingly interested in working with young talent and staging his own exhibitions.

Until recently, the gallery operated out of Lippens' home, a fifth-floor art-deco apartment in the south of Antwerp. But now, following acclaimed presentations at major shows including Matter and Shape in Paris and the Collectible fairs in New York and Brussels, Uppercut is opening a dedicated gallery nearby.

Read:

Lisbon's Estrela Basilica sets scene for Portuguese collectible design show

Lippens said he is growing in confidence with every show, as he becomes more adept at layering different scenographies.

"I've become more strict with myself, but I can also work quite fast," he said, revealing that the install of the summer show was worked out in under four hours. "There's a feeling within you; it either resonates or it doesn't."

Other recent collectible design features on Dezeen include a show in Lisbon's Estrela Basilica and our favourite pieces from NYC x Design 2026.

God Speed is on show at Chateau de Spycker, Spijkersdreef 13, 8310 Brugge, from 30 July to 30 August 2026. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world

item.content:encoded:
Interior architecture studio A-nrd has transformed a 19th-century Glasgow townhouse into a hotel with a raw, honest material palette that celebrates the Scottish city's industrial heritage.

The studio, headed by Alessio Nardi and Lukas Persakovas, was tasked with renovating the Victorian building that was originally converted into a hotel in 1999.

British hospitality brand Oberland wanted its debut hotel to reflect its low intervention approach to development, so A-nrd began by stripping away layers of additions to reveal the building's original fabric.

"From the outset, we wanted Arthouse to feel like a place that had always belonged to the city," Nardi explained. "Every decision was made with the existing architecture in mind, from restoring original features and designing bespoke furniture to collaborating with Scottish artists, makers and craftspeople."

In a previous incarnation the hotel was known as the ArtHouse so the team chose to revive this identity and reinforce the connection to the site’s history.

The reimagined interior seeks to balance the building's grandeur with a more intimate atmosphere inspired by the spontaneity and casual decor of an artist's atelier.

The original birdcage lift, stained-glass windows and tiled walls were carefully preserved and restored as part of the project, while the Victorian proportions and high ceilings lend the spaces a generous feel.

Elements such as the original brick walls and wooden floors were left exposed and any necessary repairs were made using modern materials to create an intentional contrast between old and new.

"Glasgow has a strong industrial heritage that we wanted to reference in this project," Nardi told Dezeen.

"We used materials like stainless steel, zinc and dark-toned wood to give the spaces a grittier, stripped-back aesthetic."

The 76 guest rooms combine original features with bespoke contemporary interventions such as wooden bed frames, built-in storage and handcrafted coat hooks made by West House Pottery.

The team worked with local artists, makers and organisations wherever possible, including Glaswegian glass artist Vicky Higginson, who created the wall lamps for some of the bedrooms.

The hotel's public areas include a lounge featuring a palette based around a deep-olive hue that extends across the walls, ceiling and joinery.

Bespoke seating designed by A-nrd is upholstered in a matching sage-green fabric by Kirkby Design, while vintage furniture introduces an array of different textures.

On the opposite side of the lobby, Celentano's restaurant was designed as a relaxed dining environment with a pared-back bistro aesthetic.

The reclaimed flooring, exposed brickwork and glazed tiling create a sense of consistency with the rest of the hotel, while a bespoke zinc-topped bar with a hand-hammered edge adds a crafted element.

Read:

A-nrd converts former bank into Lina Stores Shoreditch and Bar Lina

The hotel's circulation spaces combine original details with vintage furniture and custom-made elements, such as the lobby's sculptural wooden reception desk and bespoke pendant light also designed by A-nrd.

The lift and stairwell located in the centre of the building connect with large corridors where green painted walls contrast with the original white Victorian tiles and terrazzo floors.

The guest rooms were arranged across the three upper floors, while the lower ground floor, which previously housed a restaurant, is currently being converted into more compact guest rooms.

"With this project, we wanted every intervention to be guided by a desire to create a hotel that feels grounded in its surroundings," Nardi concluded.

"The result is a hotel that invites guests to experience Glasgow through spaces that feel layered, authentic and lived in."

A-nrd works across interior and furniture design, adopting an approach that focuses on the importance of storytelling and atmosphere to create distinctive, characterful spaces.

Previous projects include a similar restorative approach to the design of a hotel housed in a 19th-century mansion in south London, as well as a canalside restaurant in West London featuring hand-crafted surfaces informed by the area's industrial past.

item.content:encoded:
UK practice Heatherwick Studio has unveiled updated designs for a park along the waterfront in Louisville, Kentucky,  USA, with aspects set to be built on top of a large highway overpass.

The Belvedere park and event space connects Downtown Louisville to a section of the Ohio River waterfront. Originally developed in the 1970's, the area plays host to local concerts and events but has become "barren and disconnected" over time, according to studio founder Thomas Heatherwick.

"For more than fifty years, the Belvedere has been a stage for public life in Louisville," said Heatherwick. "But over time it's become barren and disconnected from the energy of the city around it."

The design follows a previous one revealed by the studio for the site last year.

This recent iteration centres around a large, expressive pavilion and renderings show a textured, looping pathway that travels across the site, which spans approximately 400 yards (365 metres).

"My studio's design is about restoring the buzz and sense of connection of its early years, by creating a greener, more welcoming urban heart, where everyday life can take place; from chance encounters and children's play, to festivals, performances and community celebrations," said Heatherwick.

Renderings show the looping pathway running directly into a section of the city. The pathway then curves around the main pavilion, open grassy areas, stone pavilions and down a staircase that leads onto the Louisville Riverwalk.

Read:

Heatherwick Studio designs "ribbon-like" riverfront park in Kentucky

The park also covers a large existing concrete overpass that stretches over the I-64 highway.

Foliage, trees, curved lightposts, a fountain, sculptures and amenity buildings also dot the area. The pavilion itself is also rendered from dozens of the lightposts gathered together to create a half-shell shape.

The updated design is a far cry from a previous iteration presented by Heatherwick Studio early last year. The former pictured a large, waved form covered in grass sitting atop the highway overpass.

According to local news outlet WLKY, the design was scaled back due to expense and safety concerns. The project team also launched an online survey and held community meetings late last year to get feedback on the design before making the most recent adjustments.

"Our goal is for the newly reimagined Belvedere to reflect Louisville's unique character, and bring people together again across generations, backgrounds and interests, and go on to become a place that local people proudly call their own," said Heatherwick.

Construction on The Belvedere is anticipated to begin this autumn, with an opening expected in 2030.

Other recent designs unveiled by Heatherwick Studio include a stargazing complex in Saudi Arabia and the studio's first project in Thailand.

item.content:encoded:
Artist Gregory Orekhov has created the Shadow of Light artwork by installing a black-fabric square at the Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah, USA, to show the immensity of the geology.

The temporary Shadow of Light artwork was installed and photographed in just a few hours at the Bonneville Salt Flats – a federally administered site where salt was formed by the evaporation of an ancient lake.

"When I first came to Bonneville, I was struck by its seemingly endless white surface," Orekhov told Dezeen.

"That experience became the impulse for Shadow of Light. The work was conceived specifically for this landscape. For me, it couldn't exist in quite the same way anywhere else."

To create as much contrast as possible, Orekhov ordered specialist fabric from Japan that captures 99.9 per cent of visible light and is used mostly in photographic devices that need to reduce light reflection.

The fabric was arranged in a 50 by 50 foot (15 by 15 metres) square. A stainless steel cable was inserted inside to hold down the fabric without needing to anchor it into the ground.

These cables were held to the fabric by pockets sewn into the underside.

According to Orekhov, he and his team waited for five days for the perfect conditions, wind speeds being a huge consideration in the flat, treeless environment.

Read:

Agnes Denes installs Living Pyramid in California for Desert X

The result was an "ephemeral" installation that "existed in the landscape only briefly", according to the artist.

Following in the land art tradition, Shadow of Light recalls the framing of the sky in American artist James Turrell's Sky Spaces, but in negative, with the black square putting the landscape itself into perspective, especially when seen from above.

"That is what draws me to land art," said Orekhov. "I'm not interested in physically transforming the landscape or making it submit to the work.

"I'm interested in introducing a single human gesture and seeing how it changes our perception of the entire space around it without changing the landscape itself," he continued.

Orekhov also mentioned a more personal note to the work, with the "mark" on the landscape putting his own presence and actions into perspective.

"By creating a brief mark within a space so much larger than myself, for a moment I become aware of my own presence within this immense world," he said.

"For me, nature is not a backdrop or a material but a co-author of the work."

"I can conceive a project and prepare every detail, but I cannot force it to happen," he added. "The wind, the light, the surface, and the sky remain beyond my control. Sometimes I simply have to wait for the moment when nature itself allows the work to appear."

Other recent landscape interventions include a sculpture on the shore of Finland for fish to enjoy after sea levels rise and a monumental soil installation at the Barbican by Delcy Morelos.

Photography and video by Gregory Orekhov. Video editing and score by Nikita Subbotin | Studio Landon.

item.description:

item.content:encoded:
The Canadian government's plan to restore the prime minister's residence in Ottawa highlights the chronic under-appreciation of Canadian design and its potential as a source of national pride, writes Thom Fougere.

Canadians tend to look outward for cultural validation before recognizing excellence at home. Our actors are embraced only after succeeding in Hollywood. Our musicians often require international acclaim before we celebrate them as icons. The same has often been true of our architecture and design.

And for many outside Canada, the recently announced competition to revamp 24 Sussex Drive (pictured), the building where Canadian prime ministers have lived since the 1950s, requires an explanation.

Design is rarely acknowledged as a cultural or economic force in Canada

When The New York Times recently referred to the building as "Canada's White House", it revealed something larger than the state of neglect the official residence has fallen into. Unlike the White House in the United States or 10 Downing Street in the United Kingdom, 24 Sussex has never become a shorthand for the country it represents.

As studios compete to restore the building, I am noticing how little emphasis has been placed on design as a discipline and the role it plays in shaping Canada's cultural fabric. The competition structure is open to Canadian design-build teams, but there is no similar requirement that the furnishings, lighting or materials showcase Canadian design and manufacturing.

As a designer, I often find myself thinking about these questions of Canadian identity whenever Canada undertakes significant national projects, which reflect how we see ourselves and what we choose to value. Canada is simply too vast, too geographically dispersed and too culturally diverse to produce one easily recognizable aesthetic. That diversity, I believe, is one of our greatest strengths, but it has also made it difficult to build a unified design identity or advocate for the profession with one voice.

Read:

Thom Fougere designs veiny stone tables for G7 summit at remote Canadian lodge

At the moment, Canada is experiencing a remarkable moment in design. Our furniture, interiors and industrial design have become increasingly influential cultural exports – Bocci, A-N-D Light, Lambert&Fils, Studio Paolo Ferrari, Yabu Pushelburg to name a few. More than ever, Canadian designers are attracting international attention. There is a generation of talented architects, interior designers, furniture makers and craftspeople producing work from coast to coast that stands comfortably alongside the best in the world.

Yet within Canada, design still receives remarkably little recognition.

Unlike many European countries that actively invest in design as both a cultural asset and an economic driver, Canada offers little institutional recognition for the profession. Designers often struggle to find public funding because "design" frequently falls between categories – existing somewhere between art, craft and architecture. Despite shaping nearly every object and environment we encounter every day, design is rarely acknowledged as a cultural or economic force in Canada.

Canada has no shortage of talent. What we lack is confidence in our own creative voice

Meanwhile, nations around the world have demonstrated what investment and support in creative industries can accomplish. South Korea has transformed music, film and food into globally recognized cultural exports through government-led funding and support programs, bringing its culture to the rest of the world. Scandinavian countries have built international reputations on design and architecture through collective recognition, celebration and institutional support.

These cultural industries did not emerge by accident. They were championed over long periods of time, and understood as expressions of national identity and economic force within each of their distinct countries. Montreal's recognition as a UNESCO City of Design is the best example of institutional support for design in Canada. A nationwide adoption of a similar approach for important cultural projects could create opportunities to showcase and support Canadian design, manufacturing and craftsmanship.

Canada has no shortage of talent. What we lack is confidence in our own creative voice. And this is why the design competition for 24 Sussex matters.

The competition represents more than the restoration of an ageing structure. It presents a precious chance to showcase Canadian design at every level with a nationally significant project. There is a rare opportunity here to plan and build for excellence, not to just fulfil baseline requirements – as is the approach for most institutional buildings.

Read:

"The St George's cross speaks of the power of design to transform public space"

While the current competition structure favours construction and delivery, the design community should be viewed as an equally important contributor to its success. I hope that the competition can be amended to greater emphasize the role and involvement of Canadian designers.

We can imagine a residence with interiors conceived by Canadian interior designers, furnished with pieces designed and manufactured in Canada, illuminated by Canadian lighting designers, supplied with tableware produced by Canadian ceramicists and glassmakers, and restored by Canadian craftspeople wherever existing furnishings can be preserved.

Such an approach would create more than an official residence. It could become a living exhibition of Canadian creativity and skill. It could be valued as Canadian and for its ambition by future generations.

Good design often requires a greater investment from the start, but unlike lower-cost (often imported) products built for replacement, well-designed objects and spaces endure. They can improve with age and become part of our collective cultural identity. Designing for longevity is not an extravagance. It is a responsibility that can impact both the residence and the culture at large.

We can't continue treating design as an afterthought, or an expertise that comes from abroad

Canada has never lacked remarkable and exotic materials. What we often fail to do is transform these materials into products that carry Canadian ideas. We export an abundance of raw material, but the cultural and economic value created is often captured somewhere else.

As our country imagines new public buildings, we can't continue treating design as an afterthought, or an expertise that comes from abroad. We need to recognize it as an investment in our own economy, our culture and our national identity.

Public projects should be delivered efficiently, but for one of Canada's more symbolically important buildings, efficiency alone is not enough. Design appears to be treated as one component of the project delivery, rather than as a stated objective of the competition. Projects of national significance should be opportunities to showcase and champion Canadian talent, reflecting how we see ourselves and what we choose to value.

The 24 Sussex restoration competition offers us something even more valuable than simply a renovated residence. It offers us the chance to begin believing that Canadian design is worth celebrating without needing the rest of the world to give us permission.

Thom Fougere is a Montreal-based designer working across product design, furniture, architecture and interiors. He was previously creative director of Canadian design house EQ3, is a board director of the Canadian Creators Collective (CCC) and has lectured at Harvard, the University of Toronto and the University of Manitoba.

Dezeen Showroom: Cologne-based design studio KaschKasch and brand Villeroy & Boch have released a series of hand-glazed, surface-mounted washbasins.

Adding to Villeroy & Boch's existing Antao collection, Antao Earth washbasins are shaped like dewdrops and finished with an Artisan Glaze that is applied by hand.

The finish and application technique highlights natural variations in colour and texture, according to Villeroy & Boch, and was developed with the brand's high-tech glazing lab in Mettlach, Germany.

"The challenge [with the Artisan Glazing] lay in combining an emotionally appealing, highly tactile experience with full everyday functionality", said KaschKasch co-founder Florian Kallus.

"The physical complexity in the kiln is enormous – to extend such a structure to an entire basin in a controlled and reproducible manner calls for maximum precision at the interface between design and high-end ceramics technology," KaschKasch co-founder Sebastian Schneider continued.

Villeroy & Boch intends for the basins to be mixed and matched with items from the wider Antao collection, creating a cohesive bathroom fittings scheme.

The basins are available in three different neutral, nature-informed colourways: Sand, Terra and Smoke.

item.content:encoded:
Thousands of mirrors line the gently undulating ceilings of the VISTA Science Experience Centre in Austria, completed by Dutch architecture practice Studio Maks with engineering firm Bollinger + Grohmann.

The glazed pavilion was designed as a public visitor centre to highlight the work of the Institute of Technology Austria (ISTA), providing a reception, exhibition space and cafe within a scenic park at the heart of its campus outside Vienna.

Designed by Studio Maks and Bollinger + Grohmann to feel "open and welcoming", the ground floor of the circular centre is given over almost entirely to a large cafe and shop, wrapped in full-height glass walls that are shaded by the roof's undulating, mirrored eaves.

The main idea was to create a visitor centre for the Institute of Science and Technology with a very low threshold for entry – a place where everyone feels welcome, regardless of their background or prior knowledge," Studio Maks founder Marieke Kums told Dezeen.

"At the same time, we wanted to create a space that inspires curiosity, marvel, and wonder, inviting visitors to engage with science in an open and accessible way," she added.

"At park level, the building takes the form of a circle, allowing visitors to approach it from all directions. Without a clearly defined front or back, the pavilion presents itself as an open and welcoming destination within the landscape."

At the centre of the VISTA Science Experience Centre, a circular stairwell pulls light into a basement level containing the main exhibition area. This sits alongside an auditorium, lab and workshop spaces designed for hands-on learning and experimentation.

On the southern edge of the centre, a sunken patio and curved staircase provide an external route down into this basement, which also helps to bring additional natural light into the lab area.

A largely monochrome palette was used across both levels, with white walls and black ceilings throughout the basement rooms complemented by pale oak furniture.

Above, the entire underside of the undulating ground-floor ceiling has been lined with thousands of mirrored tiles, which were designed to reflect the greens and blues of the surrounding park and sky into the interiors.

Read:

Studio Maks and Junya Ishigami create three-pronged visitor centre for Dutch park

"The roof had originally been designed as a translucent structure. However, the disruptions caused by the pandemic made this solution no longer feasible, requiring us to rethink the design," Kums explained.

"We introduced a reflective ceiling, which offered greater flexibility for the timber roof construction while preserving the intended spatial qualities of the pavilion and strengthening its relationship with the surrounding landscape," she added.

"By reflecting the park and the constantly changing light conditions, the ceiling extends the atmosphere of the landscape into the interior."

Previous projects by Studio Maks include a similarly curving, glazed visitor centre for Park Vijversburg in the Netherlands, which the studio designed in collaboration with Japanese architect Junya Ishigami + Associates.

Elsewhere in Vienna, Stephanie Barba Mendoza recently completed the interiors for an aparthotel in a 19th-century post office.

The photography is by Iwan Baan.
