Automotive brand Nissan has collaborated with London-based jewellery studio Loud Mouth LDN to create a series of custom grillz that reimagine Nissan car grills.

Designed and crafted by Loud Mouth LDN, the four-piece jewellery collection was commissioned by Nissan's Nismo division to celebrate the FIA Formula E World Championship finale taking place in London this weekend.

The grillz, which are removable accessories that snap over teeth, each feature signature design elements from Nissan's all-electric sports cars. These include the Formula E GEN3 Evo, the Z GT500, R34 Skyline GT-R and the R34 Pennzoil.

Nissan commissioned the Peckham-based studio to create the metal jewellery pieces, in a bid to combine the car brand's design heritage with London's cultural scene.

Unlike its previous commissions, Loud Mouth LDN began its design process for the collection with a focus on the "shapes and details of the cars".

"This collaboration was something completely different for us," founder of Loud Mouth LDN Reece Garcia said.

"For this project, rather than starting with letters or logos, we looked at the shapes and details of the cars and translated them into something that works as jewellery."

"Grillz are one of the only pieces of jewellery that are completely built around the individual, giving people a really unique way to express who they are," Garcia continued.

One of the pieces has a silver grill adorned with red enamel outlines and a white panel embossed with cherry blossoms, designed to mimic the exterior of Nissan's Formula E GEN3 Evo race car.

Read:

Nissan unveils electric version of 1980s Skyline GT-R sports car

Another, which was informed by the Japanese brand's Z GT500 car, has a red enamel base with black and yellow detailing to match the car's specific colourway.

Similarly, the collection's two additional pieces draw on the colourways of the Skyline GT-R R34 and R34 Pennzoil cars, featuring glossy blue and yellow-toned enamel designs respectively.

The collection will be on display at the FIA Formula E World Championship finale taking place at ExCeL London this weekend, where visitors will have a chance to win one of the bespoke pieces.

Other jewellery recently featured on Dezeen includes a quartz ring by design studios Modem and Retinaa that can prove whether its wearer is human and not an AI-generated clone, and customisable Lego rings by Studio GOGO that are "made to be played with".

item.content:encoded:
Local studio EBBA Architects has designed the first London outpost for Istanbul cafe chain Cup of Joy, using clay plaster, stone and an opaque-glass ceiling to evoke the feeling of being in a courtyard.

The studio drew on the coffee chain's founding location as inspiration for the two-storey cafe, set in central London's upmarket Marylebone area.

"The interior references the textures and tones found in Istanbul, the richness of the history found in stone walls and courtyard spaces," EBBA Architects founder Benni Allan told Dezeen.

"It is the concept of the courtyard and 'spaces between' that references the drinking of coffee, which is integral to the culture of the city and the concept."

To convey this in the 168-square-metre London location, EBBA Architects used clay plaster on most of the ground-floor surfaces and down into the stairwell that leads to the lower level.

"Clay was chosen for its innate capacity to absorb and soften: acoustically and visually, helping to do the work of calming the space," Allan said.

The studio added large slabs of Portland stone to Cup of Joy's interior, which were inlaid into the walls and then rendered over with clay.

"The stone has a block base, with it breaking up into larger and further smaller pieces as it rises; this is to give the space a sense of grounding while also being about translating the textures of Istanbul," Allan said.

"Downstairs, the clay is used on the ceilings to provide an intimate feeling, with oak panelling helping to create a calm space to relax."

EBBA Architects also filled the cafe with timber, used across both furniture and finishes.

"A datum runs continuously around the interior, anchoring guests within the room and giving the heavy walls a legible order," Allan said. "Between these sculptural elements, insertions of timber provide seating, benches, retail displays, and intimate nooks."

On the ground floor, a large oak bar cuts diagonally across the space. It sits at an angle that echoes the geometric shapes of the furniture pieces in the room to give the interior a coherent, connected feel.

Timber was also used for the ceiling, combined with opaque glass to illuminate the room evenly and provide ambient light.

This ceiling design nods to the courtyard concept that formed the basis for Cup of Joy's first London space.

Read:

EBBA founder's all-timber London apartment celebrates "alive and imperfect" wood

"The courtyard concept draws on the character and experience of being in the city, an almost civic-like space," Allan explained.

"The feature ceiling intends to bring a specific quality of light and atmosphere, like being in one of those courtyards. In addition, framed moments of light downstairs give a further sense of having glimpses of light coming into the space."

While the upstairs area has a more sculptural design and is filled with angular, geometric shapes, the basement floor features lower furniture and soft curves, as well as a circular oculus above an oak-panelled niche.

"We are interested in creating spaces that feel calm yet also provide a sense of delight," Allan said.

"A lot of our work is about using natural materials and developing palettes that are comforting on the eye and the body, sometimes unnoticed initially," he continued.

"The terracotta tones, the warm oak combined with a darker walnut colour downstairs, allow for a contrast of light and shade, which emphasises the tonality that we experienced during our research visits to Istanbul."

The studio designed most of the key furniture itself, including the shared table, smaller tables and high and low stools.

"The intention was to create objects that could follow the form of the space, including the way they help to address the shift in floor plan created by the large feature bar," Allan said.

The paper lanterns used in the cafe were also designed by EBBA Architects and are called Pulse. The studio's designs were complemented by wall lights from Danish brand Frandsen and chairs by Frama.

"Overall, there is a richness of material balanced by simple geometries that tries to create a truly unique interior environment, able to transport people to another place," Allan concluded.

"An interest in solidity and natural materials in the clay, oak woodblock and feature oak joinery helps to bring together the ethos and interests of a brand wanting to establish itself with a new identity in a new city."

EBBA Architects has previously created an all-timber London apartment for its founder and designed a coffee shop in the city as a "momentary refuge".

item.content:encoded:
Kim Kardashian has opened the London flagship branch of her apparel brand Skims, featuring voluptuous interiors by New York studio Rafael de Cárdenas.

The store is characterised by the fleshy tones that have become synonymous with Skims, the minimalist shapewear and clothing brand launched by Kardashian and Skims CEO Jens Grede in 2019.

Spread over two levels on a corner site on Regent Street, the London flagship features a wide entrance where visitors are greeted by a towering female nude sculpture by artist and frequent Skims collaborator Vanessa Beecroft.

The sculpture is illuminated by an oversized disc that was fitted into the ceiling and framed by a rounded nude-coloured partition that nods to the rest of the store's plump walls.

Rafael de Cárdenas designed a series of open-plan spaces throughout the shop, each defined by sinuous curves and shades of cream and beige.

Illuminated by another large light disc, the changing rooms have floor-to-ceiling mirrors that reflect a smooth pink pouffe and the recognisably bloated Skims logo engraved into the wall.

Throughout the store, pared-back cabinets containing apparel act as seats for cross-legged mannequins to perch on.

Rafael de Cárdenas was also responsible for the 2024 design of the Skims New York City flagship on Fifth Avenue, which follows a similar visual style.

Read:

Kim Kardashian launches inclusive Skims collection for people with limited mobility

Considering her first European bricks-and-mortar store, Kardashian said, "London has always been one of the most inspiring fashion cities in the world to me, so opening our first UK flagship on Regent Street feels especially exciting".

In 2021, designer Willo Perrin conceived the first Skims pop-up store in Paris, which featured glossy partitions and chunky changing rooms.

The same year that Kardashian opened her New York flagship store, the Skims co-founder was sued by the non-profit foundation representing the late artist Donald Judd for claiming that two pieces of furniture in the office of her SKKN beauty brand were "Donald Judd tables".

item.title: GO'C creates multi-use artist building for secluded Washington island
item.dc:creator: Jenna McKnight

item.content:encoded:
Stained cedar planks wrap a small building in the Pacific Northwest that Seattle architecture studio GO'C created for arts foundation Iolair as a gallery and live-work space for an artist-in-residence.

The building is located in Eastsound, the main village on Orcas Island – the largest of the San Juan Islands in the Salish Sea. The secluded island is reached by boat or plane.

Totalling 1,600 square feet (149 square metres), the building contains a gallery that doubles as a studio and living quarters for an artist-in-residence.

The project was commissioned by Iolair, a newly established foundation that brings artists from around the world to Orcas Island to live, work and share their creations. The artists are meant to draw inspiration from the island's "landscape and spirit".

Seattle-based GO'C was tasked with creating a building that could provide privacy for the resident artist, yet also accommodate public visits and exhibitions. The team also sought to create a building infused with local craftsmanship and artwork.

"Art and architecture are woven together throughout the project, embedding local craft into the fabric of the space," said GO'C.

The building sits on a verdant site that was once an apple orchard. The property stretches between two main roads and acts as a bridge between a residential neighbourhood and commercial corridor.

For the compact site, the architects conceived an L-shaped building that wraps a courtyard. Exterior walls are clad in ebony-stained cedar planks, with white-stained wood used along one wall to provide contrast.

The roofline is shaped to follow the transition from public to private space. Overall, the building's sculpted form responds to the functions within.

"From the exterior, the building reads as a carved mass, a solid form that has been sculpted around the requirements of its use," the team said.

Upon entering through the main door, one finds an airy gallery/studio and loft space.

On the northern end is a large circular window that pulls daylight deep into the building. Evocative of an "eagle's eye", the oculus draws upon the foundation's name, Iolair, which is Gaelic for eagle.

Beyond the gallery/studio is a small kitchen, separate public and private bathrooms, and a sleeping room for the artist-in-residence.

The outdoor courtyard serves as a gathering area and space for installations and sculptures. It is entered through a nine-foot-tall (2.7-metre) gate made of galvanised steel that was designed and fabricated by local artist Zackarya Leck.

The gate is among the many pieces by local artists. Others included a large stone sculpture by artist Pete Welty, which sits between the gallery and living quarters and grounds the space "with a sense of timelessness".

"These pieces leave a tangible imprint of local hands on the building, rooting it in the island's creative community and inviting visitors to experience art as part of the architecture itself," the team said.

Read:

Heliotrope tucks False Bay house into rocky site on a Washington island

A second building is planned for the eastern half of the site. When built, it will further "define and activate" the courtyard, said GO'C.

"Together, the two buildings will form a creative enclave, each responding to the other in form and scale, while respecting the low-rise, urban fabric of their surroundings," the studio said.

GO'C noted that Iolair was just getting established when it commissioned the design of its campus.

"Although the client had long imagined creating a place that would support artists, the organisation itself did not yet exist in any formal way," the studio said.

"Its mission and structure emerged through the planning and construction process, the architecture becoming an essential catalyst for the foundation's creation."

Other projects by GO'C include a houseboat in Seattle meant to be a study in "tiny living" and a house wrapped in concrete and darkened cedar that was designed for a family of eight.

The photography is by Kevin Scott.

item.content:encoded:
California start-up Satyress has unveiled its Threehalves robot, a teleoperated centaur-like humanoid designed to aid humans doing dangerous jobs that expose them to injury, death or extreme conditions.

Threehalves was quietly unveiled on X by Satyress founder Beau Gaston last year, who said he's been working on the robot since 2022, according to an appearance on the TBPN podcast.

The robot is designed to resemble a centaur, where its frontal human-like portion can hold power tools such as a chainsaw, while its four legs allow it to navigate tricky terrain.

According to the company, it was designed for workers such as foresters, operators, builders or craftsmen, and others who are exposed to jobs with "inhumane conditions".

"We are taking a teleoperation-focused approach not to replace skilled workers, but give skilled workers superpowers – in jobs that are dangerous for humans now, or impossible, due to risk of injury or death, extreme heat, bitter cold, pitch darkness, or other inhumane conditions," said Satyress.

The robot stands about 7 feet tall (2 metres) and is completely black, with pointed horns and small glowing eyes.

It does not have the "hands" seen on many humanoid robot products. Instead, power tools can be affixed to the robot's arms via custom, square attachments.

It is operated via remote control, with cameras in the head creating a video feed for operators.

Read:

All the cute robots that took over CES 2025

According to the company, it is "more dangerous than it looks". Some safety features were considered in its scale – the width of its horns disallows passage through standard pedestrian doors, and it cannot turn around in a standard hallway.

Certain weaker points on the body can also be pierced by a projectile or sharp instrument, which are rendered in company graphics as a gun or knife, to instantly stop the robot.

If damaged, modular components can also be replaced quickly, according to the company.

It is designed to be transported to job sites via a pickup bed, in crouched positions "side by side".

Gaston told TBPN that he embraced a more intimidating-looking design to signal to the public the humanoid robot's capabilities, rather than concealing them via a more palatable exterior.

He also said police forces have reached out to inquire about using the robot for public safety in the wake of a wave of recent publicity, which has been "surprising".

Other recent humanoid robot developments include robots designed for home environments, many of which are designed to help with household tasks such as Neo by 1X Technologies and a CLOiD by LG.

The photography is courtesy of Satyress

item.content:encoded:
A triple-height skylit atrium with a sandpit at its base sits at the heart of New Horizon, a school in Vadodara, India, designed by local architecture studio Habitat Collaborative.

Commissioned by a local chapter of non-profit Round Table India, the 1,442-square-metre building provides additional space for middle and secondary pupils at the Dr Shyama Prasad Mukherjee School.

Habitat Collaborative designed the school on a site filled with numerous mature trees, using a boomerang-shaped plan that curves to accommodate the surrounding leafy canopies.

"We wanted the design to give a sense that New Horizon always belonged to this site," principal architect Bhavik Thakkar told Dezeen.

"We carefully threaded the building between the trees such that every curve and turn of the building was a response to the surrounding foliage," he added.

"The primary facade is a sweeping concave curve, creating a welcoming gesture, inviting the kids into the building and enveloping the trees around."

The curving wings of New Horizon, which contain classrooms, a library and a science room, hug a small park at its entrance. Here, a set of steps with wavy edges sheltered by a curved balcony leads into the central atrium.

Each floor overlooks this circular atrium, which is lined by yellow-painted metal balustrades and topped by a domed skylight that draws daylight down into a small sandpit on the ground floor.

Read:

Spacefiction Studio prioritises natural light and air at colourful school in India

"The triple height atrium is the beating heart of the building, its volume a reflection of the zest and ambitions of the students," Thakkar explained.

"It floods the facility with daylight and doubles up as a thermal regulator, letting hot air escape through the stack effect," he added.

On the opposite side of the building, a garden is overlooked by a scalloped veranda edged with red stone and a balcony above, both shaded by the surrounding trees.

Inside, these curved forms are echoed in cut-outs made at the edges of the concrete floors, which allow natural light and ventilation to circulate, and in the barrel-vaulted roofs of the classrooms positioned above arched clerestory windows.

Pale yellow render covers the exterior of the school, selected as part of a colour palette chosen through participatory workshops with its students.

These also informed areas of patterned flooring made from kota stone, granite and sandstone, including a radial, triangular pattern surrounding the atrium's lightwell.

Other schools in India recently featured on Dezeen include the Shiv Nader School in Channai by Vastushilpa Sangath, which is topped by a red aluminium roof, and Spacefiction's colourful school extension with staggered courtyards and colourful skylights.

The photography is by The Space Tracing Company.

item.content:encoded:
Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla have announced plans to collaborate on a chip-building factory in Texas named Terafab, which will measure over 100 million square feet and is expected to become the largest building in the world.

Terafab is set to be built in Grimes County and span over 100 million square feet (9.3 million square metres), exceeding the current world's largest building by floor area, the 65 million-square-foot (six million-square-metre) AvtoVAZ main assembly building in Russia.

"Terafab will be epic in both its mission and in its sheer size, designed to build new compute at an unprecedented scale and speed," said SpaceX in an announcement.

The enormous factory will encompass manufacturing, packaging, and testing of advanced logic and memory devices, creating semiconductors for chips to be used in devices such as Tesla's Optimus robots and self-driving Cybercabs, as well as SpaceX's planned data centres in space.

SpaceX predicts chip demand to be "larger than the current global supply"

A render of Terafab shows a symmetrical pair of two rectangular factory wings that end in a curving roof, with a long road running through the centre.

SpaceX claimed that its and Tesla's needs for chips will exceed the world's current supply, driving the need for their own factory.

"The combined SpaceX and Tesla demand for chips is expected to be in excess of one terawatt of compute, which is significantly larger than the current global supply," said SpaceX.

"While we are deeply appreciative of our current chip suppliers, and encourage them to expand production whenever possible, this looming gulf between supply and demand is at the core of Terafab's necessity."

Read:

Stantec designs "classic American diner" for Tesla in Los Angeles

The first phase of Terafab is expected to cost $16.8 billion (£12.4 billion), and the facility will use water from the Gibbons Creek Reservoir for its industrial operations.

Once complete, SpaceX and Tesla expect Terafab to provide 3,000 jobs, with the majority of hires coming from the local area.

"We believe continued progress and leadership in space, AI, and advanced manufacturing will depend on the ability to build critical technologies domestically," said SpaceX.

"By building and operating the largest chip manufacturing facility on the planet, we're continuing down a path where future humans can compete over building the largest facilities in the solar system, and eventually the galaxy."

Last year, Musk's infrastructure firm The Boring Company announced plans for a 17-kilometre transport tunnel under Dubai, designed to link the city with speeds of up to 100 miles per hour.

item.content:encoded:
Artists and companies publishing realistic AI-generated architectural renderings in the European Union without labelling risk being fined under provisions in the EU AI Act that came into force last week.

The EU Artificial Intelligence Act Article 50, which came into force on 2 August, requires creators of realistic-looking images, audio or video to disclose if the content is AI-generated or modified to reduce incidences of harm through deception.

Many creative works are exempt from the provisions, but realistic AI-generated visualisations of buildings and interiors appear to fall under the act's categorisation of "deepfakes", according to Szymon Sieniewicz, a counsel at law firm Addleshaw Goddard.

"If it's realistic scenery with people walking around and it is AI generated, it will need to be labelled as AI generated," he told Dezeen.

Companies using AI to modify product photos, using chatbots on their homepage or publishing AI-generated text on matters of public interest will also face new obligations under the provisions.

Realistic renderings "likely" to come under deepfake definition

The EU AI Act was passed in 2024, but its Article 50 transparency provisions are the first section to come into force that affects all businesses using AI, not just those developing AI systems.

The subsection expected to have the most impact is Article 50(4), which requires creators of images, audio or video content constituting a deepfake to disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated.

While architectural visualisations might not be what most people think of as deepfakes – a term most commonly used to refer to synthetic media of real people saying or doing things they've never done – Sieniewicz told Dezeen that they are "likely" to be swept up in the act's definition.

Under this definition, an image is a deepfake if it resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful.

This includes situations where the depicted subject is fictional but realistic, as in the case of an unbuilt building or a non-existent person.

Sieniewicz said the video games industry would be facing a similar situation to architects in the case of games with realistic environments resembling cities.

The act does not dictate how AI content should be labelled beyond that it should be clear and distinguishable and relayed at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure. But guidelines in the European Commission's accompanying Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content call for the use of an icon with the text "AI generated" or "AI modified".

Violation of the act can attract fines of up to €15 million or up to 3 per cent of a company's annual turnover, but Sieniewicz stressed that he does not expect regulators to impose severe fines right away.

Product imagery and public-interest text also affected

Designers and companies showcasing their products through photography will also need to be aware of the new obligations, as any AI-made material alterations to an image will also require labelling.

For instance, Addleshaw Goddard advises that using AI to make a product appear more attractive, of higher quality or of a different colour will trigger the obligation to disclose AI modification.

Mere retouching with AI – such as cropping, colour correction, compression or replacing a background – is exempt from the rules.

There is also an equivalent obligation to disclose AI generation or manipulation for text, but only where it is published "with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest".

Read:

"Design fairs need to adopt an AI policy, and need to do it now"

General web copy is therefore unlikely to require labelling, but text related to matters such as sustainability, consumer rights and Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) strategy will, unless it has been substantially reviewed by a human.

The disclosure obligations also affect the provision of AI chatbots, such as for the purpose of customer service on a brand homepage, which is covered by Article 50(1).

Sieniewicz advises that there is no one definitive way to do this, but that the safest choice is to advise that the interaction is with an "AI-powered tool" or an "AI bot" and to make it clear in the first communication with the customer.

Other subsections in the provisions impose obligations on tech companies making tools such as ChatGPT and Nano Banana to embed machine-readable markers of AI generation into synthetic content, which users are now allowed to remove.

Provisions come at time of controversy about AI in architectural visualisation

Addleshaw Goddard advises that a lighter disclosure regime applies for artistic, creative, satirical or fictional works, but that is unlikely to apply where content is made in part for promotional purposes, such as architectural renderings and advertisements.

"There are some exemptions for artistic works, and that requires less direct transparency, but for the standard businesses in the architecture and design space, and also for product pictures, it will be the case that they need to be labelled as AI-generated," said Sieniewicz.

The implementation of Article 50 is likely to be welcomed by architectural visualisation artists, who have argued that using AI generation in place of professional 3D rendering diminishes their craft and produces error-filled results.

There has also been anger over perceived copyright violations in the training of AI systems, which are fed vast quantities of human-authored work, usually without permission, as well as worries that the use of generative AI tools may render output unprotectable and so able to be copied with impunity by others.

Top image: Hotel Attraction by AI artist Thierry Lechanteur.

item.content:encoded:
Local architecture firm RTA Studio has completed a curve-edged office building in Auckland, New Zealand, built from a diagrid structure of locally grown timber.

Situated within a regenerated wetland, the expansive, 11,500-square-metre campus serves as a global headquarters for appliance brands Fisher & Paykel and Haier Australasia, combining their offices and research facilities into a single, three-story volume.

The building's mass-timber structure was built using locally sourced pine wood and, according to RTA Studio, is one of the largest mass-timber buildings in New Zealand.

"Our response is a continuous ribbon of workplace wrapped around a protected inner landscape," studio founder Richard Naish told Dezeen.

"The loop creates an outside and an inside: protection on one side and a nurturing, biophilic environment on the other."

"We call it a groundscraper because it does everything a skyscraper does, but laid flat on the ground," Naish added.

For its mass-timber frame, the studio drew on a structural system developed by the team for a previous project – tweaking elements in response to the larger scale and complex geometry of the headquarters.

This updated structure was developed as a "digitally manufactured kit of parts" and is formed of two eight-metre-wide spans that allow ample daylight access and cross-ventilation through the building.

According to the studio, the volume of timber used for the diagrid can be grown in approximately three hours in a local plantation. Additionally, it said its structure also stores more carbon than is emitted during its construction.

This carbon-positive structure is complemented by the installation of 1,159 solar panels developed by Fisher & Paykel Home Solutions, which are expected to meet the building's annual operational energy needs.

Read:

World's tallest timber tower tops out in Sydney

"The skeleton is as beautiful as the skin," Naish said. "Its role is environmental, structural and experiential: it stores carbon, draws on home-grown engineering knowledge and creates a warm, tactile workplace."

"This is an architecture of tectonics: an architecture of parts that are clearly articulated and come together," he added.

Inside, the headquarters has been arranged around a series of three-storey atria, bridges and shared spaces.

The building's looped form was designed to create "an outside and an inside", which blocks noise pollution at its front and embraces the landscaped wetland at its centre. This is overlooked through expansive openings that wrap around the office space.

"Inside, the campus becomes transparent and opens towards a regenerated wetland oasis," Naish said. "The landscape is both environmental infrastructure and part of working life."

At one end of the building is a two-floor research and testing facility that encompasses around 5,000 square metres and is complete with lofty, industrial-style workspaces.

The facility connects to the rest of the campus through a central kitchen area that serves as a shared space for "cooking, eating and gathering" between the research and office spaces.

Throughout the interior, the building's timber frame has been left exposed and is set off in the communal areas by black timber staircases and soft furnishings.

In the UK, an office campus in central Manchester is slated to become the future home of No 10 North – the northern outpost of London's 10 Downing Street.

Meanwhile, in China, KPF wrapped a skyscraper with a one-kilometre-long series of terraces and planted staircases.

The photography is by Biddi Rowley.

item.content:encoded:
Australian designers across every discipline will be counted, for the first time, under a dedicated professional group in the upcoming census on 11 August.

The Australian Census of Population and Housing, which is held every five years, is a compulsory national population count that reveals information about the country's demographics, including respondents' occupation.

This year marks the first time that design will have its own classification. In total, 92 design occupations across 11 occupation codes will be recognised within their own dedicated occupational group: Minor Group 242 Design Professional, which sits under Sub-Major Group 24, Design, Engineering and Science Professionals.

In the country's previous classification system, design had no independent standing but sat under the architecture category,

Professions that will be counted under the new classification system include graphic designer, industrial designer, interior designer, jewellery designer, fashion designer, multimedia designer, UI/UX designer, web designer, textile designer, animator, VFX artist or illustrator.

Census will be "the first national benchmark of Australia's design workforce"

"For the first time, designers will be counted under their own professional group in the Australian Bureau of Statistics' new occupational framework, creating the first national benchmark of Australia's design workforce," CEO of the Design Institute of Australia (DIA) Simone LeAmon said.

According to DIA, the advocacy body of Australia's design industry, the design profession has largely remained invisible despite contributing an estimated $67.5 billion to the Australian economy each year.

Read:

Twelve top designers tell us how they made it

The lack of an accurate number of design professionals within the workforce makes it hard to demonstrate the evidence that will lead to industry investment and public policy-making.

"Reliable workforce data provides a stronger evidence base for government, education and industry," LeAmon told Dezeen.

"It can help inform workforce planning, skills development, higher education, migration settings, industry investment and public policy, while also strengthening recognition of design's contribution to Australia's economy and society," she continued.

Designers encouraged to identify themselves in new campaign

LeAmon believes the modernised classification framework ensures a better reflection of the diverse contemporary design practice.

"The significance isn't that Australia has finally recognised designers while other countries have not," she said.

"Rather, it modernises the country's occupational classification and, for the first time, provides a comprehensive framework recognising 92 design occupations and titles within a dedicated Design Professionals Minor Group."

To encourage designers across every discipline to identify themselves as designer in the census, DIA has created a national campaign. Called Write Designer, it features a wide variety of design projects by leading Australian designers.

The campaign was produced pro bono by creative agency Clemenger BBDO.

The projects mentioned in the campaign include the world's first modular, self-fitting hearing aid Facett, designed by Leah Heiss and Peter Blamey for Blamey Saunders Hears and the chaise lounge Lockheed Lounge designed by Marc Newson in 1986.

"Designers prove you can celebrates a profession built on challenging assumptions, solving problems and turning limitations into possibilities, and this year's census is a chance for the industry to come together, be counted and finally make the scale of that contribution visible," executive creative director of Clemenger BBDO Giles Watson said.

item.content:encoded:
Stockholm-based artist duo Bigert & Bergström has created a pink crystal-shaped sauna on a remediated industrial site in Skellefteå, northern Sweden.

Named Lithium Crystal Sauna, it is the first permanent structure completed for WasteLand Climate Action Park – a project transforming one of Västerbotten's most polluted industrial sites into public space.

After more than a century of pollution caused by toxic chemical emissions from pulp production, the Scharin industrial site underwent 17 years of extensive soil remediation work before being turned into a public park.

"Rather than erase the site's history, we wanted to build upon it," Bigert & Bergström told Dezeen. "Our ambition was to create a combination of a sculpture and a fully functional sauna."

Clad in pink titanium-coated mirrored stainless steel, the sauna has an asymmetrical faceted form made of approximately 280 prisms. The structure was designed digitally and cut with CNC machines and laser technology.

Designed to resemble an enlarged lithium crystal, it was intended to reference the mineral's role in battery technology and the transition to renewable energy.

Read:

Egg-shaped sauna creates escape for residents of Swedish town displaced by mining

"Lithium interested us because it has become an emblem of the green transition," the artists said.

"It is associated with batteries, electrification and a fossil-fuel-free future, but its extraction can also create serious environmental damage. That contradiction felt highly relevant in Skellefteå."

The structure leans backwards at an angle of four degrees, designed to appear as though it has emerged from the ground. It sits on a hexagonal wooden deck made from local heartwood pine.

According to Bigert & Bergström, its distinctive pink finish was created by evaporating titanium and condensing it onto the stainless steel in a vacuum chamber.

"The mirrored exterior reflects the river, forest and the returning vegetation, but also a landscape that has been profoundly altered by industry," the duo said.

Lithium Crystal Sauna is heated by a custom battery-operated heater. Filled with 260 kilograms of olivine stones inside a metal cage, it is clad in black flint sourced from the coast of Normandy.

"The heater was designed to operate using stored green electricity, including power supplied from standalone batteries or electric vehicles," Bigert & Bergström said.

"Although its energy system belongs to the future, the heater's form refers to humanity's oldest tool – a 2.5-million-year-old stone chopper."

In contrast to the mirrored exterior, the sauna's sculptural interior is formed from heat-resistant wood veneer over a spruce frame.

"When you enter the sauna, it's like stepping into a cave. It connects to the earliest period of human life, when we sought shelter in caves and began making fire to keep warm," the duo said.

With room for up to 12 people, the sauna is fitted with handmade alder benches arranged around the heater, while a glazed doorway frames views over the Skellefte River.

Local heartwood pine was used for the flooring, chosen for its naturally resin-rich composition, meaning it can withstand moisture and decay without chemical treatment.

"Crystal Sauna is a social and performative artwork: a place where people can gather without any of the usual social barriers and talk about changes taking place around them," said Bigert & Bergström

"We hope it will become a place that people feel belongs to them – not simply an artwork to look at, but somewhere to meet, pause and spend time together."

Other sauna projects recently featured on Dezeen include a dark and moody private sauna in New York by BoND and a sauna and tea room in Finland by Jaakko Torvinen supported by charred tree trunks.

The photography is by Pär Olofsson.

item.content:encoded:
This lookbook collates eight bedrooms and living spaces where slim-framed picture windows help landscapes become art.

A picture window is square or rectangular in shape, lacks transoms or crossbeams of any kind, has a slimline frame and comprises one singular – often large – pane of glass.

These qualities allow the views beyond to be displayed in an unobstructed way that could be mistaken for a painting hung on the wall.

The following views captured include rolling hills, dense forests, river valleys, salt marshes, desert mountains and seascapes all over the world.

This is the latest in our lookbooks series, which provides visual inspiration from Dezeen's archive. For more inspiration, see previous lookbooks featuring one-of-a-kind patios and bookmaxxed interiors.

The Blue House, Portugal, by Atelier Backlar

An expansive seascape is seen through the white-framed picture window at the foot of a bed in this clifftop house in the Azores by Portuguese architecture studio Atelier Backlar.

Rectangular and square windows punctuate the house's distinctive blue cladding, which is perched above a former traditional whaling bay below, with the Atlantic Ocean beyond.

item.content:encoded:
Tokyo studio I IN combined handcrafted tiles with an industrial-style gridded ceiling and playful animal sculptures in a store for designer Nigo's Human Made brand in Seoul's Lotte Mall Jamsil.

The lifestyle store, located inside a contemporary department store, was designed to "truly embody Human Made's philosophy, 'the future is in the past'," I IN co-founder Hiromu Yuyama told Dezeen.

To reference the past, I IN chose to clad the store with traditional Korean celadon tiles, a beloved material in South Korea.

Korea began producing celadon ceramics in the 9th century AD, with the ceramic type quickly becoming admired for its pale green colour that resembles jade, and for its smooth glaze.

"Many previous Human Made stores have been inspired by the character of existing old buildings," Yuyama said.

"Since this project was located inside a contemporary shopping mall, we sought to express the brand's philosophy through material that has been loved and appreciated in Korea for centuries, rather than through the setting."

The pale-green and blue tiles are clad in seemingly random clusters inside the 216-metre-square store, where they contrast with a light parquet wooden floor.

The patterns of the individual tiles in the Human Made shop also added a decorative aspect.

"The celadon tiles are handcrafted; each one has subtle variations in colour, and when you see up close, delicate crackle patterns – known as craquelure – become visible," Yuyama said.

"We were drawn to the powerful presence created by the clusters of individually unique tiles," he continued.

"Rather than allowing colour to dominate the experience, we wanted texture to become the defining quality of the space. From green to blue in restrained, low-saturation tones, the tiles coexist naturally with the merchandise without competing for attention."

The handcrafted tiles and the wooden floor lend an organic feel, which I IN contrasted with an industrial-style gridded ceiling that was designed to evoke factory-floor lighting.

"My impression of Human Made is embracing an industrial aesthetic, so I wanted to translate that element into the space," Yuyama explained.

"Instead of adding decorative industrial details, we wanted that character to emerge through an essential architectural element: light. We envisioned a soft, even illumination reminiscent of a factory floor."

The studio concealed the light sources above the gridded ceiling to let the light filter evenly through the grid and fill the entire space.

Playful details were juxtaposed with the pared-back, industrial materials in reference to both the Human Made brand and the department store location.

Among these are glass-encased shipping containers and a wall decoration of Human Made's heart logo, which I IN made from similar tiles but in bold red.

"The iconic Human Made heart is an exceptionally well-crafted logo," Yuyama said.

Read:

I IN uses glossy surfaces and Edo purple to create "new form of Japanese luxury" for Ginza Lounge

"Just three simple lines immediately become expressions of their unique character. There's a playfulness about exploring how far the symbol can be abstracted while still remaining identifiable – it feels very much in the spirit of Human Made," he continued.

"Since the entire space is defined by ceramic tiles, it felt natural to construct the logo using the same material."

I IN also added a number of animal sculptures to the store, which were handcrafted from veneer and foam and then painted. The sculptures were designed to resemble tanuki, Japanese raccoon dogs, as they are closely connected with the Lotte Mall Jamsil.

"Human Made chose tanuki to bring a sense of humour and liveliness to the space," Yuyama said.

"It was a reference to Lotte World, the long-established amusement park connected to the mall," he continued. "Its mascot is widely known as a tanuki, although there is a popular theory that it is actually a raccoon instead."

Japanese fashion designer Nigo launched his Human Made brand in 2010. Perhaps best known for founding cult brand A Bathing Ape, Nigo is currently designing a commercial district in Tokyo with producer Pharrell and was one of the designers of the Tokyo Toilet project.

Designing a store for a designer who is as well-known as Nigo created a "strong sense of responsibility and pressure," Yuyama said.

"However, the project gave us the space to explore new design possibilities at the same time. I believe we were able to expand the visual language of the Human Made brand while remaining true to its identity."

I IN has previously designed a light-filled beach house in Kamakura, Japan, and a department store lounge drenched in luxurious Edo purple.

The photography is by Yongjoon Choi.

item.content:encoded:
São Paulo studio Cyro Arquitetura has created a temporary studio apartment for the city's Casacor 2026 exhibition, designed to remove distractions and promote focus.

Inside an existing building in the city's historic Parque da Água Branca, the 50-square-metre installation is based on the concept of Ruído Branco, or white noise – used as a metaphor for cancelling out external distractions to induce focus.

"In a world governed by constant stimuli, the project proposes a shift — not physical, but internal. An interval. A place where excess is filtered and the essential becomes legible," said Cyro Arquitetura founder Cyro Neto.

"The space stems from the intrinsic relationship between mind and heart, highlighting how these systems operate in an integrated manner and directly influence our emotional and cognitive states. Like white noise."

The building's existing structural elements dictated the organisation of the studio, which forms an axial layout between columns below a double-height ceiling.

A low beam divides the living, kitchen and dining area from the sleeping quarters, with bourbon walnut built-in storage elements forming a portal between the two.

Original peroba wood parquet flooring running between these areas was restored, while the walls and ceiling were painted white as "a visual cleansing resource that maximises luminosity and silences noise".

A sitting area is formed by a Fita sofa and armchair designed by Guilherme Wentz, accompanied by a rare Poltroninha chair by Brazilian modernist Lucio Costa.

For dining, an Encaixe table also by Wentz is surrounded by Veadeiros chairs from Mobília Puro – all positioned in front of a stainless steel kitchen with views of the forest outside.

In the sleeping quarters, the bed rests on a low platform wrapped in caramel-coloured carpet, which features an indentation for storing books and a bedside lamp.

A custom ceramic-tile mural by Curitiba-born artist Rômulo Lass adorns a partition placed at an angle to the orthogonal floor plan.

"The intervention is a deliberate tribute to the muralist tradition that defined the identity of Brazilian buildings, especially between the 1950s and 1960s," said Neto. "The project reinterprets this heritage by bringing it to a domestic scale."

Read:

Suite Arquitetos installs rust-toned Casa Magma showroom in São Paulo

Meanwhile, the walnut storage elements incorporate a pantry, a closet, open shelving and a record player above a built-in speaker.

All of these elements are detailed to be subtle, unobtrusive and minimalist to avoid visual clutter.

"Without ruptures, the architecture creates a gradient of experience that reorganises the rhythm of the body and mind," said Neto.

"Under the design pillars of Brazilian modernism, the project is structured through the economy of means. The modern logic is to eliminate excess to highlight the essential, allowing the body to gradually slow down throughout the environment."

This year's edition of Casacor São Paulo also included an installation by Suite Arquitetos, which used Portinari ceramic tiles to create a rust-toned, residential-style show space.

During previous editions, Studio Melissa Romano got creative with fibreboard for an installation titled Casa Alma in 2021 and Studio Arthur Casas designed a prefabricated home in 2018.

The photography is by Israel Gollino.

Casacor São Paulo runs from 2 June to 9 August 2026 in São Paulo, Brazil. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

item.content:encoded:
Finnish studio AOR Architects has completed a community centre on Helsinki's waterfront, using a palette of timber and corrugated metal informed by maritime warehouses and coastal shelters.

Named Talas after a type of traditional Finnish coastal shelter, the 1,200-square-metre centre is located in Kalasatama, a former commercial port in Helsinki that is currently being developed into a residential area.

Designed for an invited competition, Talas is described by AOR Architects as a "shared living room" for the area's new community, containing a restaurant, sauna, event and work spaces.

Its shed-like form is built from glulam columns and cross-laminated timber (CLT) slabs, and topped with an oversized, corrugated metal roof, collectively resembling a warehouse that once stood on the site.

"The core idea, both emotionally and conceptually, is a shelter from the hectic urban life and maritime climate," AOR Architects founding partner Arto Ollila told Dezeen.

"One of the first new community houses built this way in Finland, Talas acts as a shared living room for local residents, combining a restaurant, event, work, and sauna facilities under one roof," he added.

Emphasising its purpose as an open, communal space, the exterior of Talas is almost entirely glazed, with half of its footprint given over to a double-height atrium. This is bookended by two double-height communal spaces overlooking the waterfront.

The timber structure has been left exposed in these spaces, with the large windows framed by timber beams and cross-bracing. Timber panels line some of the walls, with the upper sections finished with a pattern of triangular cut-outs to help control acoustics.

Read:

Assemble turns former dairy warehouses into adaptable community hub

Connecting the large, open spaces at either end are corridors finished in contrasting black timber, which lead to toilets and a series of more compartmentalised work and meeting spaces.

Between these two glazed levels are the more enclosed technical areas of Talas, which are wrapped in perforated, corrugated panels of black metal.

The timber frame of this central section extends outwards to shelter the ground floor below and create a terrace above, which sits beneath the deep timber eaves of an oversized roof.

"Materials are kept simple and ascetic to feel natural and clean – a background for life," Ollila reflected.

"Due to the harsh maritime climate, the natural wooden core is protected by a durable steel cladding and deep eaves," Ollila added.

"Bolted connections were prioritised so the timber components can be easily replaced or repurposed in the future."

Other projects in Helsinki recently featured on Dezeen include the Malmi Mortuary and Farewell Spaces by Verstas Architects, which was designed with a "comforting and gentle" palette of natural materials.

Elsewhere, JKMM Architects is currently designing the Museum of Architecture and Design Helsinki, which is set to be built on the site of the city's ill-fated Guggenheim museum.

This week on Dezeen, we reported on the demolition of a never-opened concert hall by Studio Fuksas, which is now underway in Tbilisi, Georgia.

Footage shared by local news organisation TV Pirveli captured scale-like cladding being removed from the tube-shaped Rike Concert Hall, which has sat unopened since 2012.

Demolition commenced less than two weeks after a permit for the works was issued. Studio Fuksas told Dezeen the plans were "a significant cultural setback".

Another ill-fated building to hit the headlines again was the fire-torn Mackintosh Building at Glasgow School of Art, after a campaign to save it was initiated by local architect Ruairidh Moir.

The petition asks for an independent body to take on the rebuild, after the school said it could not afford to take the project forward. It also calls on the Scottish and UK governments for financial assistance.

At the time of writing, it has 8,972 signatures. The target is 100,000, at which point it will be "hand-delivered" to both Scottish and UK Governments.

MVRDV was in the spotlight after releasing visuals of its latest proposal, Bihailou Art Village – a cultural hub in Shenzhen that will be formed of stacks of colourful volumes.

Meanwhile, author Barnabas Calder described the studio's recent competition-winning design for the green-walled Rotterdam Rocks! landmark as "a new specimen of plant-washing".

In the wake of the AI boom, we reported on the designs for two new data centres, including one in London by Morris+Company that will form part of the redevelopment of the Truman Brewery complex near Brick Lane.

The second is a "vertical data centre" by SOM for Kansas City. The 20-storey skyscraper departs from the massive horizontal structures typically associated with these facilities.

In the design world, researchers in China made waves after revealing a dress made of living mycelium that is designed to renew and repair itself.

Former Queer Eye host Tan France made his foray into furniture design, launching an 18-piece homeware collection with Singapore brand Castlery.

Projects that turned our readers' heads this week included a Passivhaus home in Hudson Valley by River Architects, a copper-clad concert hall in Evian by PCA-Stream and a cantilevered bridge in Upstate New York by SBP and Snøhetta.

item.content:encoded:
US studio Olson Kundig Architects has completed a house in the mountains of Idaho with large spans of concrete, steel and glass, topped with a retractable roof.

Known as Sky View, the 7,190-square-foot (667-square-metre) house looks out on the surrounding slopes and up to the clouds and stars over Sun Valley, Idaho.

"Sky View is very much of the landscape," Olson Kundig principal, owner and founder Tom Kundig told Dezeen.

"It harvests the visual and tangible coolness of the arroyo while framing spectacular views of the desert and mountains beyond," he added. "The design is about refining how the home opens and closes to the landscape – it brings the environment into daily life through windows, doors and even the roof."

Sky View's design offers a 360-degree view of its site, with walls that frame vistas across the mountains, meadow, arroyo and sky, allowing the architecture to step back and let the landscape be the focus.

The top of the house contains a lounge with a retractable roof operated by a handwheel, bringing occupants "face-to-face" with the sky.

"It's an all-wood room with lower ceilings, so it feels safe. But then you have these clerestory windows wrapping around the room and pulling the horizon back in," Kundig said.

"When the roof opens, you're face-to-face with this incredibly clear view of the night sky, especially in the high-desert."

The organisation of the house responds to the surrounding landscape. The side facing the arroyo – a dry creek – is closed-off with board-formed concrete, while the living spaces are elevated on the second floor with windows that look out to the horizon.

"You're moving between prospect and refuge, depending on where you are in the house," Kundig said. "From there, the house keeps reaching outward."

"The main living areas are elevated with expansive window walls, so you stay connected to the valley and the surrounding peaks without giving up that sense of security. The landscape shapes how you move through the house and how you settle into it."

The studio selected the materials to handle the home's exposed position, with concrete and steel siding that can withstand snow, wind and fire with minimal maintenance.

"Out here, the mountains and the distance between neighbors give you privacy, but they also make you more aware of the weather and the seasons," the studio said.

Read:

Olson Kundig and Erica Colpitts renovate mid-century house in North Vancouver

"Inside, the concrete walls and steel framing are softened by plaster and wood floors and ceilings. It's a mix of tough and tactile," it added.

Kundig said the design stemmed from the simple question of how one wants to live in a place like the high desert.

"This question led to an idea about connecting to the horizon line, the ground and the sky all at once," he said. "The house opens in every direction, so you're always aware of where you are. It's less about framing a single view and more about being fully immersed in the landscape."

The studio, which has offices in Seattle, New York and Chicago, employed a similar design scheme for a waterside holiday home in Sweden.

Other houses by Olson Kundig include a beachfront property with operable screens in Hawaii and a mid-century modern residence renovated with Erica Colpitts in Vancouver.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Kuryłowicz + Architects has revealed photos of the timber Arctowski Station nearing completion on King George Island in Antarctica.

Currently under construction, the three-pronged research station has a prefabricated timber structure clad in insulated golden panels.

Kuryłowicz + Architects designed the base to be a home away from home for the 28 researchers working at the Polish research station.

"The main idea was to create a 'home at the end of the world': a place that combines scientific functionality with the comfort of everyday living," said Kuryłowicz + Architects architect Piotr Kuczynski.

"The station is not just a laboratory, but a temporary home for people working in one of the most extreme environments on Earth," he continued.

"A central shared space, natural materials, and areas designed for social interaction support not only research activities but also the well-being of the residents. It is a warm Polish home protected by an intelligent outer shell, enabling people to live and work in harmony with Antarctica."

At the centre of the Arctowski Station will be a communal hub, housed in a double-height, top-lit space. It will also contain a library, gym and sauna.

According to the studio, this focus on comfort differentiates it from the majority of Antarctic research bases.

"What distinguishes the project is its ambition to bring human emotion and beauty to a place where they are least expected," said Kuryłowicz + Architects.

"Through the use of natural materials, carefully crafted interior spaces, and a strong visual connection to the surrounding landscape, the station becomes more than a piece of infrastructure," it continued. "It offers a sense of comfort, inspiration, and belonging, transforming a remote scientific outpost into a meaningful place to live and work."

The research centre was constructed from mass-timber elements that were supported on steel stilts to raise the base off the ground. It was then wrapped in a golden-coloured metal skin with extensive insulation.

This entire structure was designed to be shipped to Antarctica in 113 shipping containers and assembled within a three-month-long building window.

Read:

Eight Antarctic buildings that "have the X Factor"

"Modularity was the foundation of the entire architectural concept," said Kuczynski. "Every component had to fit inside a shipping container, survive sea transport, and be assembled quickly during the short Antarctic summer."

"These transportation constraints shaped the building's form, but they also influenced its character," he continued. "The interior, made from wood sourced from Polish forests, provides warmth and comfort while symbolically recalling the spirit of the first explorers, who carried a piece of home with them on their journeys."

"The building's metal 'skin', in contrast, represents contemporary technological achievements. Together, they create a fusion of nostalgia and 'newstalgia' – a dialogue between history and the future," he added.

Arctowski Station is the latest in Antarctica designed to withstand some of the harshest environmental conditions on Earth. These conditions largely determined the building's three-pronged form.

"Antarctica was the most important design factor," said Kuczynski. "The building had to withstand winds of up to 160 kilometre per hour, temperatures below -20° Calcius, snow, sea salt, and challenging ground conditions."

"Its three-winged form ensures access to sunlight in the most important areas, reduces snow accumulation, and elevates the building approximately three meters above the ground, allowing wind to flow freely beneath and over it, much like around an aircraft wing," he continued.

Other research bases in Antarctica recently featured on Dezeen include the Antarctic Discovery Building by Hugh Broughton Architects and NORR and a prefabricated station for Brazil by Estúdio 41.

The photography is courtesy of the Polish Academy of Sciences.

item.content:encoded:
British architecture studio Foster + Partners has been cleared of health and safety breaches after the death of a man killed by a window that fell from one of its buildings in London, following a five-week criminal trial.

The case concerned the Corniche, a tower block of luxury flats standing close to the south side of the Thames on Albert Embankment, as part of a development that completed in 2019.

Mick Ferris, a 53-year-old coach driver, was killed instantly on 2 October 2018 when he was struck by a 130-kilogram window that had fallen 90 metres from the penthouse of the building down to the street below.

The outward-opening window had been blown off its hinges with the building close to completion, the court heard. A metal restrictor to prevent that from happening had been removed.

After more than 11 hours of deliberation at Inner London Crown Court, the jury concluded that neither Foster + Partners nor the building's design engineer, engineering consultancy Wintech, should be held responsible for the death, the Guardian reported.

But the building's developer St James Group, and contractor Lindner Prater, were both found guilty of failing in their duty to keep the public safe under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 and will be sentenced on 24 September. All four defendants had denied the charges.

"An accident waiting to happen again"

The prosecution was brought by government agency the Health and Safety Executive, which had claimed the designers had ignored concerns about the proven danger posed by outward-opening, side-hung windows.

It had argued that Foster + Partners should have been aware of such risks given that glass-covered buildings are "something of a speciality" for the firm.

The designers were accused of failing to consider the "catastrophic" consequences of something going wrong with the restrictor, and of failing to take into account the fulcrum effect of an 85-centimetre-wide window coming loose.

Foster + Partners had maintained that its role in the project was limited to the visual aspects of the design, and that it had not been involved in technical matters.

The court heard that St James Group became the "principal designer" on the project in 2015, and from then on had a "duty to co-ordinate matters in relation to health and safety".

Jurors were told that in August 2017, just over a year before Ferris's death, another window panel had fallen from the same development without substantial changes made to the designs in response.

Prosecutor Gordon Menzies had said "it wasn't an accident waiting to happen" but "an accident waiting to happen again", reported the Guardian.

"It's reasonably practicable for clever people to do a simple thing and design a window that doesn't fall out once every year," he added, according to MyLondon.

Strong winds had blown the window wide open, with the oversailing glass clashing with the frame and prising off the hinges, Menzies told the court.

The court also heard that the windows had originally been designed to open inwards, but were changed to outward-openers to avoid clashing with an internal ceiling coffer containing wires and pipes.

"It had no effective failsafe, no reliable back-up. There were many things that could go wrong with the restrictors and if they did, consequences could be catastrophic," Menzies said of the outward-opening window design, per BBC reporting.

"We note the court's decision"

Following Ferris's death, the windows were changed back to inward-opening.

A spokesperson for Foster + Partners said: "Our thoughts remain with Mr Ferris' family, as they have since October 2018. We note the court's decision and are grateful to the jury for the time and care they have taken in considering this matter."

A spokesperson for Wintech said: "While the court has reached its conclusion, the tragedy of what happened remains. It is vital that we continue to reflect and learn, and as an industry, remain committed to strengthening standards and practices to help prevent such incidents in the future."

A spokesperson for St James Group said: "The death of Mick Ferris in 2018 was tragic. Our thoughts remain with his family and friends. We acknowledge today's verdict and will carefully consider its implications."

Dezeen has approached Lindner Prater for comment.

item.content:encoded:
Production designers Brandon Tonner-Connolly and Matt Hyland constructed sets including a "flesh palace" and a taxidermy-filled gas station to create a dreamlike world for this horror film starring Gillian Anderson.

The name of the film, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, nods to the lurid titles of 1970s and 80s slasher movies – a feeling the designers also wanted to evoke with the sets themselves.

The movie centres around filmmaker Kris, played by actor Hannah Einbinder, who has been tasked with reviving the fictional Camp Miasma franchise.

She travels to meet Billy, played by Anderson – the star of the cult horror film that started the Camp Miasma horror franchise – who now lives on an abandoned summer camp that featured in the first film.

Tonner-Connolly and Hyland wanted Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, which was directed by Jane Schoenbrun, to immediately draw both Kris and the audience into Billy's self-contained world on the horror-film set.

"[It's] very much supposed to be a moment where Kris is walking into this storybook world, leaving behind the reality that we've created in the first 20 minutes of the film and entering into this storybook romance," Tonner-Connolly told Dezeen.

To create a dreamlike feeling, the designers used matte glass painting, a technique of painting on glass plates that are then placed in front of the camera. This created fantastical backgrounds, such as fairytale-like mountains that sit behind the old summer camp site.

"We knew from the very beginning that the MO of this movie wasn't 'let's set out and scare the shit out of everybody,' it was 'we should take people on the best ride possible,'" Hyland told Dezeen.

Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma was mainly shot on location using two functioning summer camps on Vancouver Island, Canada.

These were turned into the summer camps seen both in the film's contemporary timeline and the 1980s summer camp of the older Camp Miasma movies.

Vancouver Island turned out to be a treasure trove of products and props, including taxidermied animals that Tonner-Connolly and Hyland used to decorate a run-down gas station.

The sourcing of these pieces ended up feeling like a horror film in itself, according to Tonner-Connolly.

"I was just driving down a road one day and saw a faded sign on the side of the road that said 'taxidermy studio' and an arrow; I pulled off a two-lane highway onto a back road and then just drove to somebody's house," he said.

"I got out and it's completely silent, nobody around, just a workshop off in the distance and a massive wood pile," Tonner-Connolly continued.

"And I was like: 'God, actually, nobody knows where I am right now – this is a very Texas Chainsaw Massacre moment'."

Other cult horror films that inspired the designers to create the right feel for the sets included Friday the 13th, Halloween and Nightmare on Elm Street.

"For this movie's approach to period and genre, it's not really about rote memorisation of accurate details – it's more about getting ourselves into the mentality of 'if we're making a slasher in the 80s, this is what we'd have available to us'," Hyland said.

Read:

Architects will "cringe a bit" at design horrors in Backrooms says production designer

However, Tonner-Connolly and Hyland also turned to the gothic romance genre to get the romantic aspect of the film right.

"We looked at Bram Stoker's Dracula and other examples of gothic romance," Hyland said. "Also Black Narcissus and Kwaidan, an older Japanese film where everything was shot on stage, even the exteriors, so it has a very heightened, storybook reality."

Some of the designs for Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma were replicated from these older films, as a nod to the inspiration and an Easter egg for horror fans.

"There was the scene where [villain] Little Death rises out of the lake, and there was a really specific life vest rack and lifeguard chair that we had seen in one of those slasher films on the beach," Tonner-Connolly said.

"We had our construction scenic department build it exactly to what it looked like in that film, and it's very subtle in the background."

Other designs were created using more modern techniques, such as the flesh wall inside Little Death's "Flesh Palace", which was a combination of visual effects and a physical wall.

"In terms of the Flesh Palace, we created a very large portion [of the wall] near where the movie slot is," Hyland said.

"That was first drawn as concept art and then turned into a 3D mockup", he continued. "From that 3D model, we were able to further illustrate the walls and figure out the undulations – how crazy are they? How veiny? And then we were able to actually export directly from there to a robot that carves that shape out of foam."

Overall, the designers focused on creating a world that would feel real not just to the film's viewers, but also to the actors as they were moving through the sets.

"We're designing for the camera, but we're also designing for the people who are in the space with us when we're shooting it," Tonner-Connolly said.

"We need to have these small details so that we can create this fully realised world. So anybody can open any drawer, anybody can look at anything, anybody can – hopefully – step into it and get lost in this bubble and create this intimate work of art."

Other film sets recently covered on Dezeen include horror film Backrooms and the Shaker-focused drama The Testament of Ann Lee.

item.content:encoded:
In this week's comments update, readers are discussing The Linhay, a family house in the Somerset countryside designed by studio Charles Gillespie Architecture.

Wrapped by a concrete colonnade, the house draws on the traditional linhay – a type of agricultural barn that is local to the region, characterised by its open-fronted form.

"Love, love, love this house!"

"This had potential, nice materials, lovely site, good references, but the design doesn't work at the level of basic proportions, composition and choice of elements," wrote Griff Ryan. "The landscape design is the nicest part."

Jessie called the project "A bit of a hodgepodge of ideas," while MKE Tom wrote, "This house has many personalities, all fighting to express themselves."

Unimpressed, JZ called it "a very upper-crusty, landed gentry vibe", while David Chase Martin said, "Even the land it sits on is embarrassed."

Though some readers were disappointed by the design, others were pleased.

"It has a vernacular banality few architects are brave enough to embrace," wrote Jb. "Well done."

Sharing their appreciation, Luke McClelland said, "A well-executed, thoughtfully designed family home. Good work Charlie."

"Love, love, love this house! Columns are a great idea and I like the differences between the facades," added Z-dog. "Great strength to the building."

What are your thoughts? Join the discussion ›

"They'll have to work harder"

Another story gaining attention this week was Decoy Font made by company Mixfont that layers two images together to trick contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots into misreading messages.

Readers shared their own experiences using the optical illusion font with different AI chatbots.

"Saved the pic and sent it to Google Gemini and it got it right on the first try," shared Fabian. "They'll have to work harder."

In response, RK said, "Odd. Did the same test on Gemini Flash Extended and it got it wrong. Also tried all the images on Claude and Gemini and they failed each time."

"I told Sol it was designed to trick it and it read it without any issues then explained it was a clever system but was easily defeatable by AI once it understood it needed to pay slightly more attention," said SgtZaddy. "It's the kind of trick that only works once, unfortunately."

Ironically, Chakras9 said, "Unfortunately, I also can't read it. I thought it said Happy Robot."

"What a time to be alive," said Bloibl . "We are already building defences against the thing we built."

To this, WJS replied, "That's different from the last five thousand years of making armour to defend against the weapons we also make how exactly?"

Have you had your say yet? Join the discussion ›

"Project of the week on Dezeen"

A project that readers could agree on was La Source Vive, a domed copper-clad concert hall in France completed by studio PCA-Stream designed "as a musical instrument".

"Project has a personality, easy to appreciate," said Marius. "However, how is the sound? With 500 seats, sound may be an issue."

Impressed, Bras Cubas wrote, "Very smart, I really like the seating and the lighting, and also the extra spaces for the technicians between the inside and outside layer."

"Looks lovely from the outside," said HP. On the same page, Design Junkie wrote, "Wow. Cool. Feels hidden away."

"Outstanding," complimented The Discreet Architect. "Project of the week on Dezeen."

What do you reckon? Join the discussion ›

Keep up to date on the latest discussions on our comments page and subscribe to our weekly Debate newsletter, where we feature the best reader comments from stories in the past seven days.

item.content:encoded:
The Royal Institute of British Architects has announced its shortlist for the Neave Brown Award for Housing 2026, which includes the expansion of a 1970s housing estate with 46 homes for social rent in London.

Also in London, a landscape-led residential development spanning five brick buildings and a 100 per cent affordable housing block bordering a woodland are among this year's shortlisted projects.

A housing complex in Glasgow combining stacked maisonettes, apartments and terraced homes also made the list.

Awarded annually, the Neave Brown Award for Housing recognises the UK's best new affordable housing. It is named in honour of British social housing pioneer Neave Brown.

The three London-based projects are Rowan Court by Satish Jassal Architects, Lion Green Road by Mary Duggan Architects with RUFF Architects and Canada Water Plot K1 by Morris+Company with White Ink.

The fourth project, located in Glasgow, is St Andrew's Drive Phases 2 & 3 by Jmarchitects.

This year's jury is chaired by associate director at Witherford Watson Mann architects Helen Lee, who praised the projects' delivery of "beautiful and enduring places to live".

"This year's shortlist for the Neave Brown Award for Housing celebrates four exceptionally high-quality affordable housing projects built in the UK recently; each reflecting Neave Brown's belief in community-focused and contextually responsive architecture," Lee said.

"The jury deliberated for some time over a very strong pool of eligible projects but were unanimous in championing the shortlisted projects," she continued.

"This year's shortlisted projects each respond skilfully to the unique urban challenges of their sites, creating beautiful and enduring places to live, supporting communities to grow and evolve," Lee added.

Satish Jassal Architects' Rowan Court oversaw the expansion of a 1970s council estate in Haringey to create 31 apartments, 11 townhouses and four wheelchair-accessible homes – all of which are for social rent.

Read:

RIBA unveils Stirling Prize 2026 shortlist

In Croydon, Lion Green Road by Mary Duggan Architects and RUFF Architects provides 157 homes between five brick buildings designed to optimise access to the surrounding verdant landscape.

Morris+Company and White Ink designed the Canada Water Plot K1 development to reflect its position beside a woodland in south east London, organising its 79 homes around a central courtyard.

In Glasgow, St Andrew's Drive Phases 2 & 3 by Jmarchitects replaces a 1960s block with a collection of 120 new homes that share a green space.

The winner of the Neave Brown Award for Housing will be announced at the RIBA Stirling Prize ceremony on 15 October in London.

The RIBA also recently announced its six-strong shortlist for this year's Stirling Prize, which includes Renzo Piano Building Workshop's cube-shaped Paddington Square. It also recently named 32 buildings the best British buildings of 2026, over half of which were in London.
