item.content:encoded:
Local interior studio Crissy Zhang Design has transformed the interior of the Parkhill residence in Melbourne, Australia, using arched forms and tactile materials to create a soft, calming space.

As part of the renovation of the 265-square-metre home, the studio redefined its internal spatial layout but largely retained the structure of the house.

"Rather than pursuing stark minimalism, Parkhill is a contemporary Melbourne residence shaped by softness, restraint and a quiet, modern Parisian sensibility," Crissy Zhang Design founder Crissy Zhang told Dezeen.

"Furniture and artworks are given room to breathe, with refinement expressed through proportion, rhythm and material control rather than ornament."

A series of arched openings was introduced to soften and reimagine the interior of the two-storey home.

According to Zhang, each arched opening was developed in response to a specific architectural constraint.

Some of these were used to conceal irregular structural outlines, while others integrate the existing structure but reshape the connection between rooms.

"What elevates the work is the degree of transformation achieved through restraint," Zhang said.

"The central idea was to re-form the house from within rather than rebuild it, transformed not by rebuilding its shell, but by carefully reimagining the architecture within it," she continued.

The communal spaces on the house's ground floor are visually linked by the arched openings, allowing for a more fluid circulation between a series of previously disconnected rooms.

The carefully proportioned openings also ensure privacy for spaces such as the study and the library, by establishing a dynamic spatial rhythm without defaulting to a generic open-plan design.

Read:

Century-old Melbourne corner shop transformed into family home

The improved visual connections and continuity across the kitchen, dining, living, study, library and bathing areas also allow natural light to move more freely through the plan.

The studio also carved sculptural niches into the thickened walls, using the same arched forms.

Crissy Zhang Design then added recessed timber shelving into the wall niches, which, together with custom-made cabinets, provide more storage space.

Tactile materials with muted tones were used to evoke a sense of grounding and quiet luxury. Limewashed walls, natural stone and pale timber were used to create a space that would feel warm and comforting.

Established in Melbourne in 2023, Crissy Zhang Design has completed a series of residential and retail projects.

Elsewhere in Melbourne, Kister Architects has turned a former 1910 corner shop into a family home, while MRTN Architects designed an extension for a house with a "collage" of forms in red-toned brick, metal and timber.

item.content:encoded:
Canadian practice Leckie Studio has completed Twin Peaks House, which features an asymmetrical roof and silvery wood cladding that helps the building "recede among the trees".

Located in North Vancouver and designed for a young family, the Twin Peaks House sits on a sloped property dotted with trees.

Local practice Leckie Studio set out to create a dwelling that felt cohesive while allowing for variety.

"The house explores how a singular formal system can accommodate different ways of living," the studio said.

"Twin House does not rely on contrast for effect. Its discipline lies in holding variation within a controlled frame."

In plan, the 3,790-square-foot (352-square-metre) house consists of two offset squares. Atop each volume are gabled roofs that slope in opposite directions, giving the house a sculptural look.

Mature evergreen trees conceal the full silhouette. Grey-hued, vertical cedar cladding further integrates the building into the landscape.

"The richness of the silvered wood allows the house to recede among the trees or emerge subtly as light shifts across the facade," said Leckie Studio.

The base layer of the home is a cast-in-place concrete plinth that accommodates the site's slopes.

A narrow walkway lined with concrete walls leads to the front door. Inside, a stairwell sits between the home's two volumes, acting as "hinge".

"From here, the house expands in one direction and contracts in the other," the team said.

"One half expands toward openness and collective use – the other turns inward toward rest and privacy."

To the west is the expansive area – an open-plan kitchen, dining area and living room.

A broad, horizontal window provides eye-level views of tree trunks and understorey. Overhead, a sloped ceiling rises gently and culminates in a circular oculus.

The other half of the house contains two bedrooms and is meant to feel more enclosed.

"The outer geometry remains consistent, yet the interior becomes more contained," the team said. "Openings are narrower and more deliberate, light is indirect."

One of the bedrooms features a circular skylight and a small loft.

"A loft occupies the apex of one gable, overlooking the living space below," the team said. "Its footprint is modest, but its position reinforces the sectional continuity of the volume."

The house also has a lower level with an office, gym, laundry room and garage.

Read:

Leckie Studio designs penthouse inside BIG's Vancouver skyscraper

For interior spaces, the team used a restrained material palette that "allows shifts in light – morning, overcast, dusk – to register without distraction".

Finishes include polished concrete floors, white drywall and oak veneers on custom millwork.

Overall, the building's design aims to "prevent symmetry from becoming inert".

"The two volumes share proportion and material language, but shifts in aperture, ceiling height and sectional organisation create distinct spatial conditions," the team said.

"Rather than expressing contrast outwardly, the project contains it within the shared shells."

Other projects by Leckie Studio include a timber-clad house in British Columbia that frames mountain views and a penthouse apartment inside a Vancouver skyscraper designed by BIG.

item.content:encoded:
Media personality and former Queer Eye host Tan France has released an 18-piece homeware collection with Singapore brand Castlery, which marks his first foray into furniture design.

France, who formerly guided fashion transformations on the Netflix show Queer Eye, told Dezeen the Castlery x Tan France Collection was informed by his British and South Asian heritage.

"I designed my current home, including some of the furniture in my home, and had the most incredible experience doing so," France told Dezeen. "Some of the items in this Castlery collection were items I wanted to make for my home but hadn't gotten to it yet."

The collection ranges from a modular Kagan sofa and an egg-like accent chair to the brightly coloured Anika table lamp and side tables informed by traditional wood turning.

Warm oak wood was used throughout the collection, along with a palette of earthy oranges and greens.

A scalloped arch can also be found in much of the detailing – a motif that France used to guide the overall collection as a nod to his South Asian roots.

"I mostly wanted to focus on a scalloped arch," said France. "It's something that is seen all over South Asia, and a muted version over all of England."

"So that was the jumping-off point, and it helped me keep the collection cohesive, as there was a clear North Star."

Read:

Pamela Anderson releases rattan furniture line informed by seaside childhood

France said he came to the design experience with ideas already in mind and that his experience in fashion design made it an enjoyable, and somewhat similar, process.

"It felt so exciting designing homeware as opposed to what I've lived most of my life designing, which was clothes," France said.

"Honestly, with such comfort with designing clothing, the design of home goods felt quite natural, as I understand fabrications, colour story and function," he continued. "It's not too dissimilar a process."

Other objects in the collection include decorative vases, a low tea table with scalloped arches etched into its legs, and wool rugs.

France says bedroom furniture may be next.

"If they have me back, I'd love to design a bed and other bedroom furniture," he said. "I'd also love to design tableware, as I'm a very keen dinner host."

The collection joins other homeware designs recently launched by celebrities who have paired up with furniture brands to help guide the design process and manufacturing.

These include a rattan furniture collection by Pamela Anderson and Los Angeles furniture company Olive Ateliers and a collection by actor and comedian Julio Torres and furniture brand Sabai, which was informed by the experience of immigrating to New York City.

The photography is courtesy of Tan France x Castlery.

item.content:encoded:
Gently curving rooflines and an asymmetrical heart-shaped stairwell characterise this multi-generational home in Ahmedabad, designed by local practices Studio Saransh and Iksoi Studio.

Named LJ House, the four-storey, 585-square-metre home was completed for a family of six on a compact urban plot, with the brief calling for an adaptable layout to accommodate changing needs.

Studio Saransh and Iksoi Studio drew upon the social and spatial principles of Ahmedabad's traditional pols – gated clusters of wooden, climate-responsive residences – maximising communal space and utilising passive cooling.

"The influence of pol houses extends beyond planning – we were interested in the underlying social and climatic intelligence of pol houses, rather than just their formal language," Studio Saransh associate partner Mansi Mistry told Dezeen.

Finished in earthy plaster with selective stone detailing, the building's form is softened by gently curving roofs along the upper levels. According to the studio, these curved roofs were shaped to reduce structural load and minimise horizontal surfaces that are likely to accumulate dust in Ahmedabad.

"As the design evolved, the curves became a way of completing the building's silhouette, breaking the rigidity of the stacked volume while preserving its monolithic character," said Mistry.

Designed around collective living, the ground floor contains an interconnected living room, dining area and kitchen that open onto a series of peripheral courtyards, extending the shared spaces outdoors.

A high boundary wall encloses the ground floor, maintaining privacy and buffering the home from street noise.

Set out in a "vertically stacked framework", LJ House is centred around a sculptural staircase that organises movement between its floors.

Designed to encourage interaction between family members, each discontinuous flight of stairs opens directly onto a shared living space, referencing the circulation patterns of Ahmedabad's pol houses. Above, an asymmetrical heart-shaped void draws daylight into the centre of the house.

Read:

SpaceDNA arranges split levels of Indian home around rust-orange staircase

"The geometry of the stairwell was almost a coincidence," said Mistry. "It emerged through the iterative process of balancing circulation, daylight and maintaining visual connections across multiple levels."

"As the stair wrapped around the central void, its changing profile naturally resulted in an asymmetrical form that resembles a heart when viewed from below," Mistry described.

LJ House's first and second floors each contain a cluster of two bedrooms arranged around a shared living space, designed to allow different generations to occupy separate floors in the future.

Bedrooms were intended to primarily be places for rest, allowing more floor space to be allocated to communal living areas.

"Private bedrooms were intentionally kept compact, containing only the functions necessary for rest," said Mistry.

"By keeping private spaces purely utilitarian, the space saved was reallocated to generous shared living areas on each floor," Mistry stated.

Throughout the interior, the architects used a pared-back palette combining muted matte finishes and continuous stone flooring, while locally sourced teak furniture introduces warmth and contrast.

"The material palette was intentionally restrained to reinforce the idea of the house as a continuous carved volume rather than a collection of individual rooms," said Mistry.

The sculptural staircase culminates in a partially enclosed roof terrace on the top floor.

Designed for Ahmedabad's hot climate, the house combines double-layered cavity walls, deep-set windows and limited openings in the external facade to reduce heat gain, while courtyards and internal voids allow for natural ventilation.

Other Indian houses recently featured on Dezeen include a courtyard house by Spacefiction wrapped in perforated brickwork and a home in Tamil Nadu by Meister Varma Architects that is built from salvaged stone.

The photography is by Ishita Sitwala.

item.content:encoded:
Dutch studio MVRDV has revealed designs for the Bihailou Art Village, a cultural development in Shenzhen, China, set to comprise a stack of colourful volumes.

Currently under construction in the Shatoujiao neighbourhood near the Hong Kong border, the 6,500-square-metre complex will contain cultural and retail spaces, including a museum and a double-height theatre, within its geometrically shaped volumes.

MVRDV conceptualised the proposal as a "vertical village", drawing on nearby homes and buildings for its assorted colours, shapes and materials.

"The joy of this design lies in its contradictions," studio co-founder Winy Maas said.

"It looks complex, but the idea of one space for every function is really quite simple."

"Though it may look like something that has never been done before, it is in fact a remix of the surrounding village: combining the colours, materials, and shapes of both its neighbours and the restaurant that once stood on this site," Maas added.

Rather than housing the programmes within one large volume, MVDRV opted for individual "houses" that could be tailored to their respective programmes.

Each volume has also been designed with its own entrance and will be connected to its neighbours via an external network of staircases, escalators and ramps.

This way, the studio explains, each programme can operate independently and determine its own opening hours.

The spaces will include a performance theatre, held within a spacious, double-height volume overlooking a plaza through a floor-to-ceiling opening.

Retractable chairs will feature in the space, allowing it to transform into an exhibition hall. Shops and restaurants will be held within the complex's smaller blocks.

Read:

MVRDV wins competition for "new world wonder" in the Netherlands

Renders of the Bihailou Art Village reveal a combination of boxy, rounded and pitched volumes finished in various types of cladding.

A landscaped plaza will wrap around its ground level, complemented by a series of "freely accessible" roof terraces atop the volumes.

"The design is imbued with a kind of civic generosity, not only in the form of its permanent accessibility and public roof terraces, but also on the ground level, where the stacked shape creates overhangs where people can shelter from sun and rain," the studio said.

MVRDV was recently named winner of a competition to design a "new world wonder" in Rotterdam, the Netherlands.

Elsewhere, the studio wrapped Beijing roof tiles around a flagship store for Urban Revivo in Beijing and topped a "polite yet radical" housing block in Eindhoven with angular roofs.

The renders are courtesy of MVRDV.

item.content:encoded:
The lily pads that float on the Kerala backwaters were the inspiration for this multi-generational apartment renovation in Mumbai by local studio The Act of Quad.

Poetically named A Borrowed Memory, the apartment is characterised by continuous green flooring designed to echo the interconnected lakes, rivers and lagoons known as the Kerala backwaters in southern India.

Priyanka Itadkar and Falguni Bhatia of The Act of Quad were drawn to the backwaters' lily pads when crafting the interior, which they said was designed to feel like "arriving at the edge of a still body of water".

This involved replacing rigid corners with curved, lime-washed walls across the home, which was renovated for a multi-generational family made up of a couple and two elderly grandparents.

Various bespoke furniture pieces in the living space were finished in subtle organic shapes, including undulating dining chairs and a door-mounted green sculpture that looks like a large curled leaf.

The studio also designed a delicate lily pad-like coffee table from clay, which was then moulded and cast in fibre. The table's jade sheen was embellished with delicate resin droplets to recall the stillness of the backwaters.

A sofa was draped in light green fabric, offering a soft antidote to an intricate hand-carved timber pillar sourced from Kerala as another homage to the state.

"Various pieces borrow the form of lily pads, but stop short of becoming literal representations," explained Itadkar and Bhatia. "The intention was never to recreate a landscape, but to allow fragments of it to quietly inhabit the home."

Elsewhere in the apartment, the grandparents' bedroom was designed to be the most peaceful space in the house, with muted tones and handcrafted timber furniture to complement the curved walls.

Rounded windowpanes, mirrors and headboards characterise multiple rooms in another subtle nod to the shape of lily pads.

The studio took care to adapt the home to fit the needs of its residents, who range in age, which included introducing a curved wall in the dining room to enlarge its adjoining bathroom to make it accessible for wheelchairs.

The younger couple's green-hued bedroom features a custom wardrobe that conceals an entire walk-in dressing space between two sliding timber panels.

In the living space, a concealed home theatre system was fitted in lieu of a permanent television on display, to encourage the sociable atmosphere of traditional multi-generational Indian homes.

Itadkar and Bhatia said that despite the modest plan of the single-floor apartment, they were determined not to compromise on standout touches including space-saving devices and bespoke furniture.

Read:

Cobalt-blue accents brighten interior of family apartment in Thane

"The reality of Indian cities is one of increasingly compact homes, and we find that challenge far more compelling than designing without limits," reflected the studio founders.

"Luxury today lies in creating spaces that are deeply personal, emotionally resonant and built around the lives of the people who inhabit them."

Founded in 2019, The Act of Quad has completed various other projects in Mumbai, including their self-designed studio in a former library and another multi-generational home arranged across a high-rise.

The photography is by Nayan Soni.

item.content:encoded:
Architect Charles Holland, academic Catharine Rossi and design studio Local Works have fabricated a table from materials harvested within a 40-mile radius of Canterbury, UK.

Named Harvest Moon, the table was designed to investigate the potential of local biomaterials, while evoking the ideals of gathering associated with harvest rituals.

"The table explores not just the materials we use but the attitudes and rituals around them," Holland told Dezeen.

"Everything comes from a 40-mile radius of Canterbury and that includes the tools that are used to assemble it, such as mallets and hammers made from apple tree wood and pegs made from chestnut wood."

The table was predominantly made from biomaterials including chalk, chestnut timbers, bark peelings, dug-up apple trees, combined with agricultural industrial waste products such as baling twine and pallet straps.

Its top was cast from chalk, along with other waste materials to form a terrazzo effect, while the legs were made from apple tree branches.

Read:

Charles Holland and RASKL add colourful contemporary bandstand to Mitcham Fair Green

"The biggest challenge was casting the top segments, the process of which involved a refinement of the technique by Local Works in their workshop," said Holland.

"The chalk was cast around a simple chestnut timber frame with embedded apple wood 're-bars' and is really a shell, rather than a solid object. The shell got thinner and the pieces lighter as the process went on due to a greater confidence in the materials."

Throughout the design, the team aimed to ensure that the materials and construction process were visible, which contributed to the overall aesthetic.

"The table is made from gathered materials and it visually expresses the ad-hoc nature of that…materials are bound together, used as supports and props or 'rebars' or as the basis of dyes or colouring," said Holland.

"The table top is cast chalk with other materials mixed in, including bark and wood chipping and baling twine, like a form of terrazzo," he continued.

"The earthiness of some parts is deliberately contrasted with brightly coloured binding which is both practical – the colours provide a key to the order in which the table is assembled – and decorative, allowing us to enjoy and express the contrasts between them."

As the table was designed as a research project, it will be disassembled and transported to various locations where it will be reassembled as a social activity.

"The core concept of the table is harvest, an idea of designing and making using gathered materials coupled with a related idea of ritual and social gathering," explained Holland.

"Each time the table is made it is a social gathering, like a barn raising."

Along with the table, the team created a publication that contains instructions and drawings of how to assemble the table, along with a musical score to accompany it.

"Each time it has been assembled the ritual changes slightly and the music evolves too," Holland said.

"The table itself is an active part of the dissemination because it will travel and its assembly involves a physical and conceptual interaction with it."

The publication also contains essays and a "guide for hosting a harvest gathering".

"We learnt a lot about the materials, about a collaborative process of design, and an open-ended one too," said Holland.

"But we also learned a lot about the processes of the two businesses we worked with, how growing, farming and coppicing is impacted by a mix of policy, economics, consumer taste, climate change and a host of other factors that are determining why our landscape is the way it is and how it is changing."

Holland and Rossi both teach at UCA Canterbury. Holland is the founder of Charles Holland Architects, which recently created a contemporary bandstand at Mitcham Fair Green and a colourful extension to a Victorian terraced house.

The photography is by Charles Holland, unless stated.
